news.title: Who’s Left?
news.text:
Republicans and pundits will play the “blame game” for a while and try to analyze “what happened” on Tuesday, November 3. And perhaps we can learn something (I doubt it). But I’m not going to do that in this article (although I just did it in a video podcast on my Substack). Tuesday’s done; it’s over, and we can’t change the results. We can try to learn from it (again, we probably won’t), pick up the pieces, and try to make sure it never happens again. And, well, it’s not like it’s never happened before. The Republicans lost 41 seats in the House in 2018, though, interestingly, they actually gained two seats in the Senate. 2026, obviously, is much worse.

So, pick up the pieces. What’s left? Frankly, not much. I’m not sure Texas is totally gone, like California and New York are, but if so, that would be very damaging. Florida is now the main Republican bulwark. What else? Well, Alabama, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma are still pretty solid (Mississippi not so much so; Georgia is gone); Tennessee and West Virginia are still strongly Republican (I have worries about Kentucky’s inconsistency), and then there are Wyoming, Idaho, and Utah that are very dependable, with maybe Montana and the Dakotas. Indiana can usually be counted on, and Missouri, too.

And that’s just about it. Republicans have about 10 “solids” and a few “usuallys.” Fifteen or so out of 50. Alaska and Mississippi may go for Democratic senators this year (it’s still undecided at this writing), but any state that repeatedly elects Lisa Murkowski as senator (Alaska) isn’t to be trusted anyway. There’s just not much left, folks, and except for Florida, the populations of all the rest of those states combined aren’t much more than California’s. Only Tennessee ranks in the top 15 in state population. In fact, let me list the top 15 states in population:

1. California: 39,355,309

2. Texas: 31,709,821

3. Florida: 23,462,518

4. New York: 20,002,427

5. Pennsylvania: 13,059,432

6. Illinois: 12,719,141

7. Ohio: 11,900,510

8. Georgia: 11,302,748

9. North Carolina: 11,197,968

10. Michigan: 10,127,884

11. New Jersey: 9,548,215

12. Virginia: 8,880,107

13. Washington: 8,001,020

14. Arizona: 7,623,818

15. Tennessee: 7,315,076

That is not a long list of states that voted Republican this year, or generally do so, and pardon my sarcasm. Yes, Mr. Trump won several of them in 2016 and 2024, but we mustn’t overlook who Trump defeated — Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. If you can find me two more…unattractive, unappealing, unpleasant, distasteful women in the United States than those two, I’d like to know who they are (they do have some competition, I admit). So, did the American people really find Donald Trump so overwhelmingly appealing that they gave him victories, or was he greatly assisted by Democratic Party stupidity?

Well, be that as it may, my point here is that only two of the top 15 states in population are reliably Republican, and one of those is number 15. And of the Western states that are “reliably” Republican, only Utah has a population over three million. Many Democratic hellhole urban areas have more people than most of the western states. Demographics are not with the Republicans here, not for the foreseeable future.

And even when the Republicans win the House of Representatives now, they get the barest of majorities and a weak Speaker. Democrats are going to have well over 250 seats in the House this term with a belligerent Speaker who hates Republicans and America. The Republicans did have 53 Senate seats the past two years; the Democrats will have at least 54 this time (two are still undecided, and right now the votes are being led by Democrats). And, of course, add several RINOs to the Democratic number. There are no “DINOs” on the Democratic Party side of the aisle. It’s not pretty.

I’m not trying to be pessimistic here; I’m just trying to be realistic. We don’t have many reliable states left, while the Democrats have many they can always count on, and those are most of the largest states in the Union. Republicans need to be trying to build some new coalitions, but…who? Unfortunately, America is moving leftward toward dependence and decadence, and those two qualities are tailor-made for Democrats.

Righteous nations do not fall; the people in such a country have the qualities and characteristics necessary to remain spiritually, morally, and nationally strong. While never perfect, America became a great nation because its people were largely spiritually and morally united. When decadence sets in, a nation begins to decline and ultimately collapse. And it’s happening rapidly in America now.

America, today, can in no shape, form, or fashion be called a “righteous” nation anymore. There are still good, godly people in the country, of course, but they are far in the minority now. No nation that lets its babies be murdered in the womb, that butchers its children for sexual purposes, that exalts sexual immorality and perversion, that doesn’t know the difference between a man and a woman, or what marriage and a family are anymore, that opens its borders and lets criminals walk the streets with impunity…no nation that allows and tolerates those things, much less has its majority political party supporting them, can be called “righteous.” Decadent, yes. Righteous, no.

When God is removed from the human spirit, the only thing that remains is an animal and a jungle. Like what America has become in too many places now, and like America elected in so many places on Tuesday. The dominance of evil human hearts is the supreme problem America now faces — in the streets and in government — and that is a problem that is exceedingly difficult to solve. How do you change the human heart?

So, after Tuesday, who’s left? Not very many, I’m afraid. But that doesn’t mean we quit fighting; it only means we fight harder.

(mklewis929.substack.com) and “Mark It Down! Bible Substack” (mklbibless.substack.com) Both free. Follow me on X: @thailandmkl. Read my western novels, "Whitewater," "River Bend," "Return to River Bend," "Allie’s Dilemma," and "Kendrick," all available on Amazon.

news.title: ‘Thank you, LA’: Nithya Raman vows to build ‘extraordinary’ future after mayoral win
news.text:
Nithya Raman, who defeated incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, has thanked residents for their support and pledged to build a better future for the city, describing her election victory as a great honour.
Raman's victory comes amid a strong showing by Indian-American politicians in the November 3 US midterm elections, with several candidates winning congressional and state-level races.
In her first statement after the victory, Raman took to X to express gratitude to voters and acknowledge her predecessor's contribution to the city.
Los Angeles, I am deeply honored to be your next mayor.
I just spoke with Mayor Bass and expressed my deepest gratitude for her leadership and decades of service. Los Angeles would not be the city it is today without her.
I love this city. I believe in its people. The work ahead will be hard, and change will take time. And together, we are going to build a future as extraordinary as the city we call home.
Thank you, LA. Let’s get to work.
— Nithya Raman (@nithyavraman) November 5, 2026
"Los Angeles, I am deeply honored to be your next mayor. I just spoke with Mayor Bass and expressed my deepest gratitude for her leadership and decades of service. Los Angeles would not be the city it is today without her," she wrote.
"I love this city. I believe in its people. The work ahead will be hard, and change will take time. And together, we are going to build a future as extraordinary as the city we call home. Thank you, LA. Let's get to work," she added.
The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with the progressive Los Angeles City Council member securing 52 per cent of the vote. Bass subsequently conceded defeat.
With her victory, Raman has become the first Indian-American and South Asian mayor of Los Angeles, the second-largest city in the United States.
Her win also means that two of the country's largest cities are now led by mayors of Indian descent. The other is New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took office in January 2026.
Raman defeated Bass despite the incumbent receiving support from prominent Democrats, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice-President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.
Her campaign was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), marking another significant electoral victory for the progressive political movement.
From Kerala to Harvard and MIT
Born in Kerala in 1981, Raman moved to the United States with her family when she was six. She studied at Harvard University before earning a master's degree in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
After completing her education, she returned to India and worked on urban development initiatives, particularly projects aimed at improving living conditions for marginalised communities.
She moved to Los Angeles in 2013, where she worked with the city's administration and became involved in efforts to address homelessness. She also helped establish the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition in 2017.
Raman entered electoral politics in 2020, defeating incumbent David Ryu to represent Los Angeles's fourth council district. She was re-elected in 2024.
Her mayoral campaign took an unexpected turn after she withdrew her initial support for Bass's re-election bid and entered the race in February, just hours before the filing deadline, Al Jazeera reported.
Housing, homelessness at the centre of campaign
Raman campaigned on changing what she described as Los Angeles's "broken status quo", promising to address the city's longstanding problems.
In her victory speech, she pledged to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.
"For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do," she told supporters.
Her key promises included expanding affordable housing, tackling homelessness, improving neglected public services and repairing roads and infrastructure.
She also proposed deploying more medical teams to assist people experiencing homelessness and called for a different approach to the city's housing crisis.
Raman further pledged to protect residents from immigration enforcement efforts, safeguard Hollywood jobs amid industry cuts and improve neighbourhood facilities.
Her victory comes at a challenging time for Los Angeles, which continues to deal with a homelessness crisis, infrastructure concerns and the aftermath of the devastating January 2025 wildfires.
She will also have to prepare the city for the 2028 Olympic Games, which will bring additional demands on its infrastructure and public services, Aljazeera reported.
In a statement on Thursday, Bass congratulated Raman and said she was committed to ensuring a smooth transition.
Thank you, Los Angeles. Serving as your mayor has been the honor of my life. https://t.co/ObC2zrVao9
— Karen Bass (@KarenBassLA) November 5, 2026
“Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles. You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me. She added, moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote.

news.title: Gavin Newsom Messed Up
news.text:
The midterms are over, and eyes are turning to the 2028 presidential race. Gavin Newsom — who led the betting odds to be the next Democratic presidential nominee from Donald Trump’s 2024 election until August of this year — had imagined that this would be his moment. 

Alas, right now, everyone is turning their attention to younger candidates, such as Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. In the case of Ossoff, he feels like a breath of fresh air to Democrats in comparison to Newsom and his scandals. Ossoff’s first and only wife is a beautiful doctor, and he has two young daughters. He is politically talented and only 39 years old. (RELATED: 2028 Begins!)

Newsom, on the other hand, has a list of scandals that leaves a bad taste in Democrats’ mouths, all of which I chronicle in my book, Newsom Unleashed: The Progressive Lust for Unbridled Power.

He was married to Kimberly Guilfoyle, who is now the face of alleged MAGA corruption. He had an affair with a young mother, Ruby Rippey, who was in the throes of addiction to cocaine. (Recently, she revealed in Vanity Fair that she was blackout drunk during some of their sexual encounters.) He dated a teenager while mayor of San Francisco. He has admitted to being at his mother’s bedside when she was illegally euthanized. He holds responsibility for California’s homelessness epidemic, as well as numerous other crises in California, from the highest cost of living in the nation to the highest unemployment rate in the nation. (READ MORE: Newsom’s Affair Partner Reveals She Was Blackout Drunk During Encounters)

There’s so much more. He rose up in San Francisco politics as the playboy adopted son of Gordon Getty, and his companies were bankrolled into existence by Getty. He had problems with alcohol as mayor. He aroused national hatred for dining at the French Laundry while telling his citizens to wear masks between bites of food. (RELATED: Gavin Newsom’s Pandemic Regrets Tour) 

There’s more. Newsom was the No. 1 defender of the cognitively addled Joe Biden. Even after the disastrous debate in which Biden revealed he had lost it, Newsom decided to travel around the country to convince Democrats to stick with Biden. (RELATED: Gavin Newsom Breaks With Biden to Set Up Presidential Run)

Newsom’s former chief of staff — who served in that office from 2023 to 2024 — has pleaded guilty to three federal charges related to schemes she was part of while she occupied that office, and she has stated that the feds under Joe Biden tried to get her to implicate Newsom in wrongdoing.

And now, Newsom and his wife are under federal investigation. That investigation is drawing headlines and attention, as recent news reports reveal that some of the investigation centers on the funding of his international travel. Newsom claims it’s all an effort by Trump to prevent him from seeking the White House, but Department of Justice sources have assured media outlets that the investigation is very much legitimate and serious. (READ MORE: The Feds Are Closing In on Newsom — and His Corporate Bankrollers)

Why on earth would Democrats go with this man? At some point, all of this is just too unpleasant for donors and voters to swallow.

I realized Newsom had messed up when he launched his memoir in February of this year and embarked on a major media tour to sell it. There was a Vogue puff piece, a New York Times profile, and a nearly 4,000-word New Yorker profile. He was starting his campaign way too soon. His plan had been to try to get his scandals dealt with and out of the way before the election began, but the end result is that he seems stale and like last year’s news. 

When his book came out, I said, “But this is all way too early. The public only has so much appetite for following any candidate’s moment in the spotlight. If Newsom tries to manufacture another moment for himself a year from now, Americans will be too bored to pay attention.”

“He’s wasting political capital when few Americans care,” I said. “And worst of all, as the frontrunner, he’s painting a giant target on his back and inviting fellow Democratic hopefuls to shoot.” (READ MORE: Gavin Newsom Will Regret His Book Launch)

Democrats have also gotten annoyed with Newsom’s obsession with himself, seeing in it echoes of Trump’s own egomania. In January of this year, David Axelrod complained publicly about Newsom’s “self-puffery.”

Newsom was leading in the betting odds to be the next Democratic nominee until he was passed by Ocasio-Cortez in mid-August, according to Kalshi. Right after the midterm elections, Jon Ossoff garnered significant hype and jumped to a 26.3 percent chance of winning the nomination. Newsom, meanwhile, fell to being tied with Ocasio-Cortez at a 13.6 percent chance of winning the nomination. Meanwhile, the New York Times average of the 15 most recent polls on the Democratic primary race puts former Vice President Kamala Harris in first place with 34 percent support and Newsom in second place with 20 percent support. He is followed by Pete Buttigieg, Ocasio-Cortez, and Ossoff.

News reports are now beginning to say that some Democrats have soured on Newsom.

Page Six published an article Thursday claiming, via anonymous sources, that Democratic insiders say donors “may have tired” of Newsom.

The source said, “He seems to have peaked too early.” According to Page Six’s account, this is because people are talking more about Newsom’s affair with Ruby Rippey and the federal investigation into him and his wife than his presidential campaign.

“All of a sudden, Gavin Newsom with all his drama doesn’t seem as appealing as Beshear or Ossoff,” the person said.

Meanwhile, a different source told Page Six: “The media loves him because he’s good copy. But I am amazed how the donor orbit is over him. His moment is in the past. There’s baggage and then there’s Titanic steamer trunks of baggage. Let’s not forget he was married to Kimberly Guilfoyle, and the state of California is such a mess.”

Indeed, last month I wrote that Newsom would likely have to spend his entire campaign explaining why he married the woman who is “a living caricature of a corrupt, morally bankrupt MAGA woman” in the eyes of Democrats. (READ MORE: Gavin Newsom’s Awkward Marriage to Kimberly Guilfoyle) 

But never underestimate Gavin Newsom’s ability to rise from the ashes after a horrible scandal. There’s been scandal after scandal in his nearly 30 years in public office, and he is still at the top of the national conversation.

Donald Trump is an instructive case that voters can look past personal baggage, improprieties, and political scandals, and that these can, in fact, give interest to a candidate. Trump is also a case study in how prosecutions pursued under the leadership of the opposite party can backfire. Trump’s second term in office is, after all, a direct result of the prosecution by New York District Attorney Alvin Bragg.

Newsom is still a darling of the Left. For example, Vanity Fair’s October edition features a thousands-of-words-long profile of the California governor and his preparations to pursue the presidency. He has a huge base of donors behind him, and he has made himself out to be the Democrats’ top opponent against Trump. He has been preparing for this moment all his life.

Never underestimate Newsom’s ability to rise from the ashes, but, at some point, Democrats must get sick of him.

Ellie Gardey Holmes is the author of Newsom Unleashed: The Progressive Lust for Unbridled Power.

news.title: Who is Harmeet Dhillon? The Indian-origin lawyer exiting Trump's administration after a rocky tenure
news.text:
Harmeet Kaur Dhillon, an Indian-origin Republican lawyer who led the US Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, has resigned from her position and plans to return to the private legal sector.
Dhillon stepped down on November 5, ending her tenure as Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights. She was nominated by US President Donald Trump in December 2024 and confirmed by the Senate in April 2025.
Her resignation comes amid a major political shift in Washington following the 2026 midterm elections, in which Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress.
Dhillon is a prominent conservative lawyer and political activist who has spent years representing Republican politicians, campaigns and organisations in legal disputes involving free speech, civil liberties and constitutional rights.
Serving my country as AAG for Civil Rights has been the honor of a lifetime. We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more. I want to thank President Trump for giving me this opportunity. I look forward to what’s next!
— AAGHarmeetDhillon (@AAGDhillon) November 5, 2026
Who is Harmeet Dhillon?
Born in Chandigarh, India, Dhillon moved to the United States with her family at a young age. She grew up in New York and North Carolina before pursuing a career in law.
She graduated from Dartmouth College with a degree in Classical Studies before earning her Juris Doctor from the University of Virginia School of Law in 1993. During her time there, she served on the editorial board of the Virginia Law Review.
After graduating, Dhillon clerked for Judge Paul V. Niemeyer of the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit. She subsequently worked at several corporate law firms before establishing her own practice, Dhillon Law Group Inc., in San Francisco in 2006.
Her firm handles commercial litigation, free speech disputes, political law and civil liberties cases.
In 2018, she also founded the Center for American Liberty, a conservative nonprofit legal organisation focused on civil rights litigation.
How Dhillon became a prominent Republican figure
Dhillon gradually built a strong presence in Republican politics, holding several leadership positions within the party.
She served as chair of the San Francisco Republican Party and vice chair of the California Republican Party. She also represented California as a Republican National Committeewoman from 2016 to 2025.
Her legal practice brought her into contact with prominent conservative politicians, political campaigns and public figures, representing clients in disputes involving constitutional rights, media and free speech.
In January 2023, Dhillon made a bid for the chairmanship of the Republican National Committee (RNC), challenging incumbent Ronna McDaniel.
Although she did not win the position, the contest raised her national profile within the Republican Party.
Dhillon's role in the US Justice Department
Trump nominated Dhillon to lead the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division in December 2024. The US Senate confirmed her appointment in April 2025 by a 52-45 vote.
She became the first Republican woman and the first Republican of Indian origin to head the division.
The Civil Rights Division is responsible for enforcing federal laws protecting people against discrimination in areas including employment, housing, education, voting and access to public services.
A controversial past, a turbulent tenure
Dhillon has rarely been far from controversy, facing political and legal scrutiny at several stages of her career.
Before joining the government, she drew criticism from fellow Republicans over her past association with the ACLU and political donations to Democrats, including Kamala Harris. Her 2023 campaign for RNC chair was also reportedly dogged by a whisper campaign targeting her Sikh faith. Meanwhile, her law firm represented prominent conservative clients in contentious cases, including legal challenges to the 2020 US election results.
But her time as Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division from 2025 to 2026 brought the sharpest scrutiny. Dhillon reshaped the division's priorities, directing its resources towards issues favoured by conservatives, including corporate diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes, municipal gender policies and access to state voter registration data. The changes triggered fierce criticism and deep internal turmoil, with more than 75 per cent of the division's career legal staff reportedly leaving during her tenure.

news.text: Harmeet Kaur Dhillon, an Indian-American lawyer who served as assistant attorney general for Civil Rights and headed the US Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, has resigned, marking the first departure of a senior administration official since the US midterm elections.Dhillon's exit comes after a controversial tenure during which the division underwent a sweeping change in priorities, moving away from several investigations into police practices while pursuing cases involving diversity policies at universities, admissions practices and allegations of antisemitism on campuses.Attorney General Todd Blanche announced her departure on X on Thursday, praising her leadership and saying she had defended the civil liberties of Americans and enforced the law "without fear or favour".Dhillon, however, maintained that the decision was entirely hers and had been made weeks before the elections. Speaking to Fox News Digital, she said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles had requested that she delay the announcement until after Election Day. "My decision, my choice," she said, adding that she wanted to return to the private sector.In a separate post on X, Dhillon described her time in office as "the honour of a lifetime", highlighting her role in advancing the administration's position on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and women's sports."We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls' sports, and so much more," she wrote, thanking Trump for the opportunity.Her tenure was marked by a sharp reduction in the division's workforce, with more than three-quarters of its staff at the beginning of Trump's second term leaving the department. Dhillon welcomed the departures, describing them as the "biggest single personnel self-purge in DOJ history".The changes also drew strong criticism from former Justice Department officials, who accused her of weakening the division's traditional role in enforcing civil rights protections. Stacey Young, a former division attorney who now leads a network of Justice Department alumni, called Dhillon "the most destructive, lawless and hateful" head of the division in its history.Before her appointment, Dhillon had built a profile in Republican politics and conservative legal circles. Her San Francisco-based law firm represented Trump in several legal battles, including a dispute involving the congressional investigation into the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol. She also unsuccessfully contested the Republican National Committee chairmanship in 2023.Born in Chandigarh into a Punjabi Sikh family, Dhillon moved to the US as a child after her parents left India. Her father was an orthopaedic surgeon, and she has spoken about her parents' decision to settle in America as a defining moment in her life. She became a naturalised US citizen at the age of 10.Dhillon's resignation adds to the list of Indian-origin figures who have held prominent positions in American politics and public service. Dhillon's departure comes amid the growing presence of Indian-origin Americans in senior positions in US politics and public service. Other prominent names include Vice President JD Vance's wife Usha Vance, FBI Director Kash Patel, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya and former White House AI adviser Sriram Krishnan. The community has also had a significant presence in the Democratic establishment, including former vice-president Kamala Harris, former US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy and former White House domestic policy adviser Neera Tanden.You use AI every day. Her leadership was marked by a reorientation towards diversity initiatives and university admissions policies. Attorney General Todd Blanche endorsed her efforts to uphold civil liberties, yet faced pushback due to workforce reductions within the division. Dhillon's exit also reflects a growing trend of Indian-origin leaders shaping American governance.

news.title: Trailing MAGA Republican begs for recount cash: ‘Costs money every single hour’
news.text:
Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith's (R-MS) campaign is appealing to donors to cover legal costs as she trails Democrat Scott Colom in Mississippi’s Senate race, Politico reported on Thursday.

Mississippi and Alaska are the last two uncalled Senate races, Politico reported, and both parties are raising money for possible recounts, although control of the Senate is already settled. Hyde-Smith is behind Colom by under 2,000 votes with over 95 percent of ballots in. In Alaska, Sen. Dan Sullivan trails Democrat Mary Peltola by a little over 600 votes with roughly three-quarters counted.

Both these results in red states would be political earthquakes if they hold.

A Thursday email from Hyde-Smith’s campaign said legal fights across the state demand major resources and that having lawyers monitor ballots and defend the seat “costs money every single hour,” according to Politico. The Senate Republicans’ campaign arm set up a recount fund on Election Day, adding Sullivan first and Hyde-Smith by Wednesday morning.

Democrats are fundraising as well. Colom’s campaign launched a legal fund, and Politico reviewed emails on his behalf sent to the lists of the Democratic National Committee, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Gov. Wes Moore (D-MD), Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA), and others.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris sent her own appeal, writing that Republicans “will not let another go without a fight.”

Politico says what happens next is unclear. Alaska counts slowly and uses ranked-choice voting, so if neither Sullivan nor Peltola reaches 50 percent in the first round, tabulation is expected in mid-November. Mississippi has no legal provision for a recount, automatic or requested, so court action would likely come first.

The Trump administration tried to sue Alaska before the election over the presence of another candidate with the same name as Sullivan, but this suit was dismissed.

news.title: Who Is Nithya Raman? India-Born Democratic Socialist Who Defeated Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass
news.text:
India-born Nithya Raman, a relatively little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in a stunning electoral upset, setting the stage for a significant political shift in the country's second-largest city.
Raman's victory represents a generational change in Los Angeles politics, following a similar trend in New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor last year. However, unlike Mamdani, Raman did not attract widespread national attention during her campaign and sought to establish herself as a candidate willing to differ with her own progressive political camp on certain issues.
The 45-year-old urban planner entered the mayoral contest after a dramatic reversal, having initially backed Bass, who was once her political ally. Raman eventually announced her own candidacy shortly before the filing deadline, arguing that the city had reached a "breaking point".
Bass' defeat makes her the first Los Angeles mayor in 20 years to lose a re-election bid. Her tenure was significantly affected by the deadly Palisades Fire, which broke out while she was overseas and caught the city's fire department unprepared. The destruction and its aftermath left many residents holding the mayor accountable, dealing a blow to her chances of securing another term.
Raman Promises Changes In Policing, Basic Civic Services
Raman's rise comes amid growing divisions within the Democratic Party, with left-wing challengers increasingly taking on establishment candidates across the country.
Among her key campaign promises is the removal of Los Angeles Police Chief, whom she considers too accommodating towards federal immigration authorities. She has also pledged to address the deterioration of essential civic services, with residents grappling with pothole-filled roads, damaged sidewalks, unclean neighbourhoods and non-functional streetlights.
Raman was also critical of Bass' handling of homelessness, describing the incumbent's efforts as ineffective. She has proposed a different approach that would involve expanding medical teams working with people living in homeless encampments and on the streets. The aim, according to her plan, is to establish trust with homeless residents and eventually help them move indoors.
Her proposals also include increasing the availability of housing to relocate people currently accommodated in hotels rented by the city as part of its homelessness response.
Raman has said her strategy could bring down the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when Los Angeles is scheduled to host the Olympic Games. However, homelessness has remained a persistent challenge in the region despite billions of dollars being spent to address the crisis.
Homelessness, Public Safety Among Voters' Top Concerns
Raman's campaign gained momentum amid voter dissatisfaction over problems that have continued to affect Los Angeles during Bass' tenure. Bass, 73, faced a challenger who positioned herself as the candidate of change in a city struggling with longstanding civic issues.
A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted between October 19 and 25 found that approximately four in 10 likely voters wanted reducing homeless encampments to be a top priority for the next mayor. Around three in 10 identified public safety or the construction of more affordable housing as key concerns.
Raman also managed to counter Bass' criticism that she was "not ready for primetime" and lacked the experience required to govern a city with a population of 3.8 million.
Her campaign focused heavily on the city's unresolved problems and questioned Bass' leadership. In one advertisement, Raman highlighted several troubled locations, including the site of a massive warehouse fire last summer, the homeless hub of Skid Row and shuttered shopping centres and storefronts.
"Our city is in crisis," she said in the advertisement, which showed an empty lectern. "Where is our mayor?" Raman asked.
Bass, meanwhile, maintained that her administration had made sufficient progress to deserve another four-year term. She also attempted to portray Raman's positions on policing and homelessness as "extreme".
Raman Wins Despite Limited Support From Democratic Establishment
Raman's victory came despite receiving considerably less backing from prominent Democratic leaders than her rival. Bass enjoyed the support of California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. Almost every member of the Los Angeles City Council also backed her campaign.
Before becoming mayor in 2022, Bass had served in California's state Legislature and the US Congress. She had also been considered as a potential running mate for former President Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election.
Billionaire real estate developer Rick Caruso, who lost to Bass in the 2022 mayoral contest, also signalled his preference for the incumbent this time. Although he did not formally endorse her, Caruso publicly said he would vote for Bass, an important indication of support from the business community.
Raman, on the other hand, secured backing from several advocacy and political organisations, including Our Revolution, established by Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. However, her campaign had relatively few endorsements from influential local politicians.
She also held a widely publicised private meeting with former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, who did not take an active role in the mayoral contest. The meeting indicated Raman's efforts to widen her political network beyond her existing support base.
Building a broader circle of political and business allies could prove important as Raman prepares to govern a city with diverse economic interests. Los Angeles is home to a major port, leading universities and research institutions, a prominent entertainment industry and a substantial tourism sector, all of which present distinct challenges for its incoming administration.

news.title: New York’s 5 Costliest House Races Draw $308M in Spending
news.text:
New York congressional races drew a staggering $308 million in spending during the 2026 midterm campaign, including roughly $64 million in the Empire State’s most closely watched battleground.

The contest for New York’s suburban 17th Congressional District in the Hudson Valley generated $64 million between a fiercely contested Democratic primary and the general election. The total includes spending by candidates’ campaigns and political action committees.

About $22 million was spent during the Democratic primary, in which military veteran and eventual winner Cait Conley defeated Beth Davidson and Peter Chatzky, according to campaign finance records. Outside groups also poured $30 million into the swing district, which encompasses portions of Westchester, Dutchess, Rockland and Putnam counties, filings show.

On Tuesday, Conley unseated two-term incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler, who had won reelection in 2024 even as Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris carried the 17th District.

The spending pushed the race far beyond the $38.4 million spent in New York’s 19th Congressional District in 2024, which was then the most expensive general election contest on record.

Several high-profile New York City primaries also ranked among the year’s most expensive contests, including the Manhattan battle to replace retiring Rep. Jerry Nadler in the 12th District.

Democratic candidates and the groups supporting them spent $56 million in that race, records show. Super PACs, including Jobs and Democracy PAC and Think Big, accounted for the bulk of the spending, with $43 million invested in the contest.

Those groups received substantial backing from artificial intelligence companies and their leaders, who spent heavily in the June primary as concerns about the emerging technology resonated with Democratic voters. Democrat Micah Lasher ultimately won both the primary and the general election.

The race to succeed North Country Rep. Elise Stefanik in the 21st District was the third-most expensive overall. It included a bitter primary between eventual Republican nominee Anthony Constantino and GOP Assemblyman Robert Smullen.

Constantino went on to win a nail-biting general election against Democratic dairy farmer Blake Gendebien, despite Stefanik carrying the district by more than 20 points in each of the previous two cycles.

The Democratic-aligned House Majority PAC made a seven-figure advertising buy in the week before Election Day. Constantino, an Amsterdam-based chief executive of a sticker and decal manufacturing company, meanwhile invested $17 million of his own fortune in the race.

Democratic socialist star Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez faced no serious reelection challenge in the 14th Congressional District, but $26 million was still spent on the contest, making it New York’s fourth-most expensive House race.

Ocasio-Cortez, who is openly considering a presidential or Senate bid in 2028, had $18 million cash on hand as of mid-October.

The fifth-most expensive contest was the $20 million showdown in New York’s 3rd Congressional District between Rep. Tom Suozzi, D-N.Y., and former Assemblyman Mike LiPetri, records show.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, like Ocasio-Cortez, faced no competitive challenge but still spent $19 million, according to filings.

Left-wing Democratic socialist challenger Darializa Aviles-Chevalier’s primary defeat of Rep. Adriano Espaillat in the 13th District ranked as the seventh-most expensive race, with approximately $15.4 million spent, records show.

news.title: Mississippi, Alaska Senate Races Remain Too Close to Call
news.text:
Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska remain too close to call as Democratic challengers cling to slim leads.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom has a narrow lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, an unexpected development in a reliably red state.

The razor-thin margin surprised political experts as Mississippi has long been a Republican stronghold. It came alongside other surprising Democratic wins in the American South.

Alaska’s Senate race also remains unresolved, with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola hanging on to a 637-vote lead over Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, according to The Associated Press, with 74 percent of ballots counted.

As of Nov. 5, Colom held a 1,145-vote lead on Hyde-Smith, according to the Associated Press, with 96 percent of the vote counted.

That’s in a state President Donald Trump won in 2024 with 60.9 percent of the vote, defeating Kamala Harris by 22.9 points. Hyde-Smith won reelection in 2020 over Democratic challenger Mike Espy by a 54 percent–44 percent margin.

Matthew Dallek, a political science professor at George Washington University, told The Epoch Times that the economy, the war in Iran, and high gas and grocery prices contributed to the tight race.

Dallek said the switch was a perfect storm where black voters supported Democratic candidates in Mississippi while Latino voters came out in full force to elect Democrats in Texas after members of the two demographics helped elect Trump in 2024.

“So this is true across the South. Like, very large African American turnout, which is part of a response to the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and a response to maybe Trump gutting affirmative action and all kinds of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and civil rights measures,” Dallek said.

He was referring to the U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling on the Voting Rights Act and gerrymandering in April. A majority said Louisiana’s Senate Bill 8, which created a second majority-black district, was racial gerrymandering and unconstitutional. Critics, however, warned it would have far-reaching impacts for voting rights.

University of South Florida political science professor J. Edwin Benton told The Epoch Times that southern voters were once part of a “solid Democratic South” before a shift to conservatism in the 1980s and 1990s in the Deep South and Florida.

The rise of Trump and the Make America Great Again movement solidified Republican support in states such as Mississippi and South Carolina.

The midterms changed the political alignment, with Democrats making gains in traditional Republican states, including Texas, Iowa, and Kansas.

Benton said voters who were once captivated by Trump turned out in force due to the rising cost of gas prices and groceries and being at war.

Vice President JD Vance posted on X that low voter turnout was not the problem, saying many people who voted for Trump and Vance in 2024 turned to Democrats in 2026. He said the war in Iran, the cost of living, putting America first and the change in relationship with Israel were the reasons Republicans lost.

In Florida’s 14th Congressional District, longtime Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor fended off Republican challenger Mike Beltran.

Despite a redrawn district, Benton said Castor won because she has delivered on promises over her nearly 20 years in office.

The Alaska Senate Race has proven to be tighter than Mississippi’s, as Peltola has a slim lead over Sullivan in another state controlled by Republicans.

In Alaska, if neither candidate gets 50 percent or more of the votes, rules call for a ranked-choice tabulation, where voters would rank their choice in order of preference.

The trending results are a far cry from the incumbent Sullivan’s previous run in 2020, when he won his second term by more than 12 points over nonpartisan candidate Al Gross.

But Peltola has proven to be a formidable challenger as votes continued to be counted in a normally Republican-controlled state.

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit to segregate and review ballots cast for independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan, asserting that his appearance on the ballot created confusion with Sen. Dan Sullivan.
news.summary: Other surprising wins have emerged in the American South.

news.title: What Midterm Blue Tsunami Could Mean for 'Frozen' Housing Market
news.text: Democrats' midterm victory could bring a new wave of housing legislation to Washington as Americans continue to struggle with high home prices and elevated mortgage costs. The housing market today has left many prospective buyers and sellers on the sidelines. In Home Depot’s most recent earnings call, CFO Richard McPhail said America is facing “frozen housing market conditions.” However, now that Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections, prospective homebuyers are hopeful the tide could turn. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer outlined a five-part housing agenda earlier this year focused on lowering rents and increasing homeownership, and new congressional majorities could give Democrats the ability to turn some of those ideas into legislation beginning in January. Why It Matters The housing affordability crisis has increasingly become a problem for both buyers and sellers. High mortgage rates have made monthly payments considerably more expensive for prospective buyers, while existing homeowners with much lower rates have had a financial incentive to stay put rather than sell and take out a new mortgage at today's higher rates. The resulting "lock-in effect" has contributed to unusually low turnover and inventory. At the same time, years of inadequate construction, particularly of lower-cost starter homes, have left the country facing a persistent supply shortage. What Does the Democratic Midterm Win Mean for the Housing Market? In the short term, there will probably be fewer changes than prospective homebuyers might hope. Congress cannot simply order mortgage rates lower or force homeowners with ultra-low pandemic-era mortgage rates to sell. Democratic control does, however, change which housing bills will receive committee consideration and floor votes. It could also put housing near the front of the new Congress' affordability agenda. “Democrats are in favor of affordable housing, but they are also in favor of regulation, so that is a double-edged sword,” Kevin Thompson, the CEO of 9i Capital Group and the host of the 9innings podcast, told Newsweek. “Some believe regulation is one of the causes of lower production of affordable homes, given the profitability of building larger homes. There will need to be a constructive approach to bringing incentives and supply into equilibrium.” After the election, likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats were "laser-focused on addressing the affordability crisis that has been crushing everyday Americans." And there is reason to think housing could produce more actual legislation than some other Democratic priorities. What New Housing Proposals Could Democrats Pursue? Build More Homes Increasing supply is likely to be central to practically any Democratic housing agenda. Schumer's Opportunity Starts at Home agenda explicitly calls for more housing construction, alongside policies to address rents and large corporate investors. “No matter where you live in America, no matter if you’re a Republican, Democrat or independent, everyone worries about housing affordability,” Schumer said previously. “When the rent or the mortgage is too high, you can’t afford much else. It squeezes every other aspect of your life.” Democratic Senators Amy Klobuchar, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Tim Kaine also introduced the Housing Supply and Affordability Act this year. The bill would establish a competitive federal grant program for states, cities and regional planning agencies developing housing strategies. Invest More Federal Money in Affordable Housing Beyond just increasing supply, progressive Democrats could push Congress considerably further. Representative Yvette Clarke of New York introduced the Affordable Housing and Area Median Income Fairness Act of 2026 alongside Representatives Rashida Tlaib, Ayanna Pressley and Joaquin Castro. The legislation would authorize $5 billion annually from fiscal 2026 through 2035 for the HOME Investment Partnerships Program in high-housing-cost areas, another $5 billion annually for qualifying Community Development Block Grant assistance and $5 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund. However, getting Trump to approve that level of new federal spending would likely be considerably more difficult than reaching an agreement on regulatory changes. "Any federal action may fall victim to a divided government, as any new bills will have to gain the support of the White House to ultimately be approved," Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor for the University of Tennessee at Martin, told Newsweek. "Still, the Trump Administration has signaled in the past a willingness to entertain ideas for bringing new housing costs down, so there may still be some middle ground that can be found." Help First-Time Buyers Get Into Homes Democrats may also revisit assistance directed at the buyer rather than the builder. The best-known recent Democratic proposal came from former Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign, which proposed providing up to $25,000 in down-payment assistance to eligible first-time homebuyers and enhanced assistance for first-generation buyers. Harris' broader housing agenda also called for building 3 million additional homes, providing tax incentives for builders of starter homes and expanding existing affordable-housing tax incentives. Target Institutional Homebuyers Democrats have also focused on the role large institutional investors play in the housing market. Schumer's housing agenda included a pledge to confront what he described as predatory corporate practices. On this topic, Democrats may find an unexpected area of agreement with the White House. Trump issued an executive order in January aimed at preventing large institutional investors from acquiring single-family homes that could otherwise be bought by families, and his administration has called on Congress to codify that policy into law. “Proposals like cracking down on predatory lending practices and increasing federal investment in low-income housing could do a lot to help,” Thompson said. “I think with control of the House and Senate, they could work to lower tariffs on lumber and steel, which could directly impact the cost of producing homes.” Could Democrats Actually ‘Unfreeze’ the Housing Market? Democrats could do many things to impact the housing market. They could increase federal housing investment, offer incentives for communities to remove barriers to construction, and even provide tax benefits to builders or buyers. However, it’s unlikely they could ‘unfreeze’ the housing market on their own. That’s because they don’t have the power to shift the interest rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage. So even an aggressive housing package would probably take years to significantly expand supply. Buyer subsidies could provide faster relief to individual households, but without additional inventory they would risk increasing competition for the homes already available. “I think the housing market is in a bit of a stalemate at this time, given the fact that rates will remain stubbornly high and housing prices won't come down,” Thompson said. “However, federal budget deficits have often fallen or grown more slowly under Democratic administrations, partly through tax policy. If that trend continues, you could see some money redirected toward housing from other areas of the federal budget.” What Happens Next Democrats will take control of Congress in January. At that point, the housing proposals floated during their campaigns can begin turning into actual legislation. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant, Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Now that Democrats won control during Tuesday’s midterm elections, prospective homebuyers are hopeful the tide could turn.

And I think that we expected it to be–you know, all of us who were warning against it dragging on and that the president needed to bring it to a conclusion one way or another before the election. You know, I think this result is an indication of that. But to pretend that that’s the only issue, that’s absurd.

When you see the overwhelming opposition in both Republican and Democrat districts to data center policy across the country, you can’t pretend that’s not an issue. If you see that kind of reaction that you had within the suburban vote to the ICE enforcement issue, for instance, that is something that is obviously an issue, and the fact that House Republicans and Senate Republicans alike never came up with a feasible or realistic, communicable affordability agenda is ridiculous and absolutely absurd. I mean, I can’t believe that they never developed a response in any way, shape, or form to DSA candidates basically saying that they were going to pay for things with, you know, the leprechaun money.

And then the last thing that really sticks out to me about this election, and it’s infuriating to me: the Democratic Party has, for decades, used the power of the government and the bureaucracy to take taxpayer money and to send it to people who quite often do not deserve it, or to whom it is illegal to send that money. They have been doing that repeatedly, over and over again. And we’ve discovered that, to a great degree, in part thanks to the vice president, but others as well, in states across the country. And yet, the Democratic Party was somehow able to use the combo of the Epstein files and various deals and crypto mishegas, and, you know, Russian oligarchs and the specter of this, that, or the other to make the corruption argument something that worked in their favor. That’s political malpractice. It’s absolutely absurd that that happened. And wasn’t it kind of self–

Guy Benson: In fairness, wasn’t some of that self-inflicted by the Trumps?

Ben Domenech: Yes. I mean, I think that one of the things that really, you know, sticks out to me about all of this is that I think there are a lot of people who do not understand that when the American people look at Donald Trump… and they hear arguments about his corruption or the like at this point, you know, especially after so many years of knowing him, their response is he’s a billionaire. He’s not going to be bought. He is not somebody who can actually, you know, sort of be manipulated this way. But for the people around him, that’s not true. That doesn’t play the same way. And I think that a lot of the times there were people who were simply tone deaf about the way that this looked to the American people. And especially in an election in which people have economic concerns that are very real and affordability concerns about the issues that are affecting their life, and they see a kind of Gilded Age approach in Washington, DC, where people are partying, throwing around their weight, and doing deals with all sorts of, you know, shady figures and that kind of thing, it was going to have a backlash.

In this context, you remember 2006 because you and I have been around long enough to have seen that kind of thing play out when it came to scandals for House Republicans. The scandals back then were also about corruption, but they were of a different kind, but it was the same kind of play, which happens, you know, when people get–they get fat, they get happy, and they start playing the Washington game of thinking everyone takes money from all these lobbies. Everyone, you know, does these kinds of deals. Why shouldn’t I too? And that has consequences at the ballot box. And I think a lot of Republicans ended up bearing the price for those types of deals, whether they were party to them or not.

Guy Benson: Yeah, and the thing is I’m not trying to pile on the vice president because I think some of what he put out there is correct and he’s talented in many ways, but you know, in his big post-mortem explanation, the corruption thing–unmentioned, because I think he can’t really bring that up for these reasons. And you know that that is something that would not fly certainly with Trump and some of the other people, like that would seem like in some ways a validation of those attacks. He did not mention tariffs. I think it was not just the policy of the tariff, but also just the absolute confusion around it and the rollout and that crazy chart and then the picking fights with friends. I just think a lot of people were like, what is going on? This seems crazy. He’s not prioritizing the cost of living for us. There’s some other priority here. Tariffs did not come up in this long post that he put out, but he boiled his entire argument down to this sentence, quote, “the reason we lost is the war.” He had a lot of other caveats and things like that, but his core argument was the reason we lost is the war.

Ben Domenech: And then he got President Trump. I understand you don’t want to pile on the vice president. I’ll pile on the vice president for you. JD Vance is the least popular vice president in modern history. Keep this in your mind, OK? He’s less popular not just than Kamala Harris; he’s less popular than Dan Quayle, he’s less popular than Al Gore, he’s less popular than Mike Pence, he’s less popular than Joe Biden. By the way, the most popular vice president in the modern era is Dick Cheney, which is hilarious. But I just think that, look, this is the thing: you know what is in common with all the people that I just mentioned? Joe Biden, by the way, didn’t run as vice president. He had to have that interim four-year period before he ran. None of those people other than him became president.

He just wants to ignore the things that he likes that damage the party, that damage Republicans across the country. I’ll give you–I mean, here’s just one example of this: I think that the Iowa Senate race would have gone very differently if the president hadn’t decided at the very last, you know, sort of stages of things that he needed to go against America First policy, screw over every rancher who actually deals with cattle in America, and import cheap Argentinian beef to try to band-aid over the problems with beef prices in America. Okay. That’s a perfect example of a situation where, you know, I think that you could have had a Republican from Iowa if not for that. You know, Ohio was supposed to be a red state; it’s not. There are tons of different examples of this.

And I think that the problem for the vice president is his connection–and I truly believe this, I’ve been arguing this is going to be a problem for him when it came to just, you know, hands down winning the next nomination–his connection with Silicon Valley and the tech community is going to be a drag. If you had any questions about that after this election, I think that they have been thoroughly resolved. People are concerned about AI. They’re concerned about data centers. They’re clearly concerned about it in a bipartisan way. And the Republicans don’t really know or have an answer to that question. Neither do Democrats, by the way, but they get away with demagoguing it. The situation that I think is there is one that he is not prepared to navigate. He has not in any way acknowledged that it was a drag on this because he knows the president is all in for it. And I think that that’s, you know, it’s a very intellectually weak argument, and I believe failed on the facts to say that this is just about the war.

Guy Benson: I agree with that piece, and I was contradicting some of the things that he asserted in his post yesterday in some detail to open the show. I also just think, OK, so he’s not willing to cross Trump on some of these other issues–corruption, tariffs–and it might just be stuff that he happens to, you know, and tariffs like he might agree with the policy, maybe not; the AI stuff, I get that. If you’re the loyal vice president, you don’t want to be, you know, criticizing obliquely or directly the boss or major policies. But he’s making a big exception on the war, saying this is the reason we lost at the exclusion basically of all others. You know, there were different factors, like he had some of that throat clearing, but quote, “the reason we lost is the war” is the nut of this whole thing.

This coming on the heels of right before the election, Vance being asked about whether Trump would endorse him for president. I just feel like, obviously, it is a precarious spot to be Donald Trump’s vice president. Ben Domenech: They do not. Because, you know, I don’t think any other president, any other candidate for president, by the way, would have picked somebody who was a senator who, you know, had served a year and a half, by the way, when taking a chance. He seems to want to create some kind of distance. That didn’t play out well for Al Gore; I don’t think it’s going to play out well for him.

I’m offended by that disloyalty. I’m offended by the fact that the vice president of the United States thinks that he can just go out there and say, “Well, I’m going to have my own message now, because this is now about me.”

Guy Benson: Well, I mean, especially because it’s also too clever by half, because he’s trying to camouflage it all as like, “Oh, well, some data people told me this,” and it’s like, it’s so obvious, and Trump is clocking it, right? Trump obviously knows what is happening here. I think Vance thinks it’s subtler than it actually is.

Ben Domenech: So, I mean, that’s a good question, Guy, and I actually–I don’t know, if he thinks that, then that’s a gigantic mistake on his part because the president’s a smart guy. He knows the ways that this game is played. Okay? I mean, he used to be–I mean, one of the things, remember Trump used to be the biggest kind of leaker about himself to the major papers in New York. Yeah. He would build himself up, you know: “sources close to Donald…”

Guy Benson: Yeah, no, he thought he was like, “I’m totally anonymous, but I’ve got a great scoop about the…”

Ben Domenech: “…the amazing Donald Trump.” But the thing that I–it’s hilarious, but the thing I think is truly going on here is that the vice president wants to create distance in a situation where he cannot possibly create distance. He’s going to be the vice president. Presumably, I mean, unless he like resigns in a huff tomorrow over the Iran War, which I’m sure, you know, many, many podcasters would rejoice.

Guy Benson: But yeah, but how many voters would? Ben, very quickly, just one minute here: personnel changes. Rubio rumors, those have been swatted down today by the State Department; the Hegseth stuff swirling. 30 seconds.

Ben Domenech: I have been predicting for a while that I thought he would be kindly asked to leave after this election, simply based on the fact that after ’06 Rumsfeld was fired. But I–by the way, I don’t necessarily think that he deserves that, but I do think that the president’s going to make some heads roll. I got to be honest: I think the person who actually needs to get fired is Brooke Rollins for the kind of ridiculous things that have come out of the Ag Department and the idea that we should buy chicken instead of steak. It just sticks in my craw. Guy Benson: –some of that Senate stuff, so okay. All right, we’ll be watching. We’ll keep tabs on these things. Ben Domenech, Fox News contributor, thank you so much. Great to be with you.

news.title: Karen Bass out as L.A. mayor, as voters pick DSA-backed Nithya Raman
news.text:
Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation's second-largest city.

The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at city hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign. 

When she takes office next month, Raman will join the vanguard of democratic socialists in municipal government. In addition to Mamdani, Janeese Lewis George was elected Tuesday as mayor of Washington, D.C., and Katie Wilson is mayor in Seattle. 

Asked about the success of democratic socialists in mayoral contests, U.S. President Donald Trump said "we'll see what happens" but warned the impact of the changes they make might be irreversible.

"There'll be a point at which if people are unhappy, they'll be changed," Trump said in the Oval Office. "But unfortunately, usually that happens so late that you'll never be able to bring back a city or a country or a state. You know — when it goes too far."

Raman's entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, who was once her ally. She said the city had reached a "breaking point" and announced her own candidacy just before the filing deadline.

Bass calls to congratulate victor

Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," Bass said. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us."

Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for re-election. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered. 

As votes were being counted earlier this week, Raman delivered an election night speech Tuesday that marked a campaign coda, summing up voters' frustration with a city that seemed to be adrift, and her vision for the future.

"For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do," she said. "L.A. stopped being a place where we could build things, where we could open things, where we could film things, where we could create things."

She said she would restore "that ambitious Los Angeles, that joyful Los Angeles, that creative Los Angeles, that entrepreneurial Los Angeles."

Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.

Raman wants police chief ousted

Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities. 

She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years, leaving neighbourhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights. 

Raman called Bass's efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She's promising a new approach on the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors. 

Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless. 

She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region. 

Raman offered change

Raman, 45, was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under Bass, 73. 

A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about four in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about three in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.

Reality star Spencer Pratt out of L.A. mayor's race as progressive Nithya Raman advances

She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was "not ready for primetime" and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.

"Our city is in crisis," she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicentre of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. "Where is our mayor?" Raman asked.

Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman's views on policing and homelessness as "extreme."

Top Democrats backed Bass

Raman's victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former U.S. vice president Kamala Harris and former U.S. House speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the city council. 

Bass served in the state legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former U.S. president Joe Biden's running mate in 2020. 

How AI has helped a former reality TV star become a contender for L.A. mayor

In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.

Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians. 

She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle. 

Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that's home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions, and serves as a major tourist destination.
news.summary: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation's second-largest city.

news.title: Ex-Biden official projected to win bid to unseat Mike Lawler in high-stakes House race
news.text: A former Biden administration aide is projected to defeat Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., in one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 election cycle. Cait Conley, a military veteran who served on the White House National Security Council, will likely be coming to Congress next year after beating the two-term incumbent for the job, The Associated Press projected late Thursday. Multiple forecasts suggested the seat would be a likely pickup for Democrats. THUNE WEIGHS NIGHTMARE SCENARIO FOR GOP AS DEMOCRATS THREATEN TO FLIP HOUSE Both parties poured enormous resources into the race for New York’s 17th Congressional District in the months before Election Day. It was widely seen as key to both parties’ quests to win the House majority. The district, which sits just north of New York City, was won by Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. TENSION ERUPTS DURING HOUSE MIDTERM DEBATE AS LAWLER FACT-CHECKS NEW YORK DEMOCRAT OPPONENT ON IMMIGRATION Lawler spent much of the race walking a political tightrope between supporting President Donald Trump and positioning himself as an independent voice. And the race itself was marked by bitter divisions on issues like immigration enforcement and taxes. DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST Among Lawler’s backers were the parents of Sheridan Gorman, a college student from his district who was killed in Chicago while she was out with friends. Gorman’s accused killer is an illegal immigrant who was previously arrested for shoplifting, but was released without a federal immigration detainer because of Chicago’s sanctuary city laws. Lawler and Gorman's parents have pointed to her killing as proof that Democrat-backed sanctuary laws — which are active in New York as well — are deadly for Americans. He argued that Conley would do nothing to mitigate the effects of illegal immigration. ARMY COMBAT VETERAN CHALLENGING MIKE LAWLER CALLS HEGSETH NATIONAL SECURITY 'HAZARD,' BACKS IMPEACHMENT Conley, for her part, condemned Gorman’s killing and has said she is against illegal immigration, but she has not spoken out against sanctuary laws specifically. Fox News Power Rankings rated the district as "lean Democrat," while the Cook Political Report ranked it a toss-up.
