news.title: Dispatch From Dearborn: How El-Sayed Flipped Precincts That Had Voted for Trump
news.text:
As the sun set in Dearborn, Michigan — a city on Detroit’s western border that is often called the “capital of Arab America” — the sense of urgency to elect Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate was becoming palpable on an unseasonably warm November election day.

The lines of hijab-wearing women and curly-haired young men at the polling stations on November 3 kept growing longer. More cars clogged up the streets around the schools that were serving as election precincts in normally quiet neighborhoods.

“Today, our vote is our power,” said Fares Alshawhati, an Arab American truck driver who was urging voters outside of a polling location to back El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate.

Now, election data shows that Arab voters in Dearborn needed little convincing to elect El-Sayed. The progressive former public health official approached 100 percent support in some of the most predominantly Arab precincts in the city. 

It was a stunning swing in a community that had all but abandoned the Democratic Party two years ago over Israel’s wars on Gaza and Lebanon.

A Dramatic Rebuke to Trump and the Republican Party

In one precinct in Dearborn’s Southend neighborhood, which is home to a large Yemeni community, more than 97 percent of the voters — 927 out of 949 — cast their ballots for El-Sayed. Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers received less than 2 percent of the votes in the Southend.

In 2024, Republican President Donald Trump won the same precinct with nearly 53 percent of the votes. His Democratic opponent, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, finished a distant third behind Green Party candidate Jill Stein. Harris received less than 13 percent of the votes. 

That’s an 84 percentage point shift from Harris to El-Sayed among voters in the same precinct in two years.

And such shifts did not only occur in this one precinct. Across Dearborn, voters swung by dozens of percentage points in a dizzying political whiplash in anger at Trump and his policies.

El-Sayed won Dearborn with 82 percent of the vote. In predominantly Arab precincts on the east side of the city, support for El-Sayed surpassed 94 percent. 

“I think that shift is very healthy actually because it indicates that the community is not a monolith and also that the community is moving where the country’s best interest is,” said Chadi Abdulrazek, an Arab American political activist who was volunteering to help elect El-Sayed.

“Two years ago, we were deep in a genocide,” Abdulrazek told Truthout. “This community was bleeding. We were all hurt. We were all seeing our families being slaughtered. We were all in pain for a long period of time, and the Democratic Party failed to stop that genocide.”

He added that Trump came and made big promises about being a man of peace, and some Arab Americans decided to give him a chance.

“Eventually he failed and made things worse. I think it is actually very smart to see that the community and people across the country are shifting their perspective because they’re seeing what has happened in the past two years,” Abdulrazek said.

Arab American voters interviewed by Truthout in Michigan consistently cited three reasons for backing the Democrats in this election cycle: Trump lied to the community about his foreign policy; they support El-Sayed’s policies, such as Medicare for All; and they were turned off by Republicans’ embrace of Islamophobia.

In the lead-up to the election, many Arab voters criticized Trump for breaking his promises about pursuing peace in the Middle East and for starting yet another destructive war in the region, while also continuing to offer unconditional support to Israel, even as it intensified its abuses in Gaza and the West Bank and sought to annihilate South Lebanon.

El-Sayed’s platform of ending funding to Israel and investing in local priorities also aligned with the community’s agenda. And his being Arab and Muslim further boosted his standing. 

El-Sayed’s campaign manager, Alia Kapasi, hailed his gains in the Arab community, releasing a statement on November 5 saying: 

In 2024, the Democratic ticket performed poorly with Arab-American voters in Dearborn. Abdul didn’t just make up those losses, but ran up the score. Record-breaking turnout in Dearborn was nearly 5% above 2024 turnout. While Harris lost the city by 6%, Abdul won by more than 65%. In Dearborn, nearly 3,700 more voters voted in the Senate contest than in the race for Governor.”

Kapasi also paid a nod to El-Sayed’s dominant performance in neighboring Dearborn Heights, which is also home to a large Arab community.

A Statewide Victory Against Overt Anti-Muslim Bigotry

In order to win the senatorial race, El-Sayed was forced to overcome extreme and persistent targeting for his Muslim identity: Rogers and Trump had made El-Sayed’s faith a focal point of their campaign in Michigan. 

Trump repeatedly called the Democrat a “jihadist,” as Rogers falsely accused him of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas, and Hezbollah.

Voters were flooded with misleading ads on the subject. 

One Republican-funded video commercial featured a woman in a burqa and baselessly suggested that El-Sayed would impose Sharia law if elected, warning that under Islamic rules, women cannot leave the house without a guardian. 

In her November 5 statement, El-Sayed’s campaign manager, Kapasi, underscored the bigotry against him, saying: “The Republicans made a targeted choice to use Islamophobia as their core line of attack against Abdul, and it backfired tremendously with one of the key constituencies that won Trump the presidency in 2024.”

In 2024, Republicans had softened their tone on Arabs and Muslims, seeing an opening in a community that was furious at Democrats over then-President Joe Biden’s uncompromising support for Israel.

According to estimates by the Arab American Institute — which corrects for undercounting by the U.S. Census — Michigan is home to nearly 400,000 Arab residents. In a state of 10 million people, that bloc of voters can be decisive. 

So back in 2024, Trump and his team decided to woo them. 

He personally visited Dearborn, spoke of peace, and invited Arab American supporters and local Muslim imams to the stage in one of his rallies.

The Republican president ended up winning Dearborn that year, and his staunchly anti-immigrant adviser Stephen Miller thanked the city on election night.

The honeymoon, however, was short-lived. 

On his first day in office in 2025, Trump revoked U.S. sanctions against violent Israeli settlers. Weeks later, he called for removing Gaza’s entire population from the Palestinian territory and turning it into the “Riviera of the Middle East.”

While some may have given Trump the benefit of the doubt, the war on Iran — which he launched jointly with Israel earlier this year — left few Arab Americans in Dearborn on his side.

Then came Trump and Rogers’ Islamophobic campaign against El-Sayed, which pushed what remained of the local community’s Republican voters to the Democratic camp.

Trump had especially angered the Yemeni voters who backed him in 2024 after revoking temporary protected status for Yemeni immigrants earlier this year. More recently, the U.S. president called Yemen and other developing nations “shithouse” countries. 

Abdulrahman Barman, an activist in Dearborn, said the Yemeni community had discussed ways to respond to the president’s comment and decided not to release angry statements. 

“We concluded that the best response is through the ballot box — that we must all come out and vote, so our response is direct and practical,” Barman said. 

In the mostly Yemeni Southend neighbourhood, turnout comfortably surpassed 2024 levels despite presidential elections usually drawing out more voters than the midterms. 

After the polls closed on November 3, dozens of Arab Americans flocked to an election results watch party at a banquet hall on the east side of the city.

Celebrations began even before the results started to trickle in. The high turnout was enough reason for joy.

“Two years ago, the Republican Party and Trump came to Dearborn and … they bamboozled the Arab community and gave us false promises,” journalist and activist Hussein Hachem told the crowd. “But they don’t know the Arab community. The Arab community doesn’t forget. Today, the Arab community in Michigan and across the nation gave Trump a slap in the face that he will never forget for the rest of his life.”
news.summary: Voters who spurned the Democratic Party in 2024 turned out en masse to elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

news.title: Inside the NYC Members' Club Where Republicans and Democrats Party Together
news.text:
Since its founding two years ago, The Bench has hosted insiders ranging from CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Monthly dues, “just to keep the lights on,” run as little as $50. The space is regularly used for events unaffiliated with The Bench: readings by literary magazines, climate week pop-ups, splashy debates. Michka Bengio, the social club’s owner and co-founder, is an earnest believer in dialogue and, if his programming is any indication, a little bit of a chaos agent. He likes to produce scenarios that underscore political tensions, like when he had Weiss’s The Free Press, co-host a watch party for Mamdani’s 2025 election. According to those who attended, it was a somber evening for the pro-Cuomo crowd, though some of them nevertheless returned to The Bench for this week’s midterms viewing.
On the night of the midterm elections, partygoers had the option of viewing the election results in a spacious, orderly room displaying CNN’s broadcast or in a lounge-y, narrower space screening Fox News’s coverage. In a cozy hallway between the two screens, guests could buy cocktails and popcorn or engage with people whose political views differ from their own—arguably The Bench’s most exclusive offering.
“There’s just a whole splatter of different opinions that come in here,” says David Azoulay, who works with the content agency Fixer Media. “The Free Press, the Manhattan Institute, and then I also get to meet a lot of people who are working in the Democratic space, on the Biden or Kamala Harris campaigns.” Azoulay helped produce events for an “America 250” tour in collaboration with Young America’s Foundation, a conservative youth organization, and has worked with provocateur Ben Shapiro and former Prime Minister Boris Johnson. Though he used to be a registered Democrat, he “grew up” and now identifies as a proud Republican. While Azoulay engaged in a playful back-and-forth with a progressive 21-year-old over what he considers to be the fallacy of socialism, Democratic councilmember Christopher Marte milled about wearing an “I Voted” sticker.
Over the sound of people screaming about the James Talarico-Ken Paxton race, Marte told me he met Bengio 10 years ago through Arena, a New York-based political organization that took off in the wake of the first Trump presidency. “It was all these young people trying to figure out how to get involved in politics. A.O.C. was on the couch, Alessandra Biaggi, all these people who were just curious, post-Trump election,” he says. At the time, Bengio was working as a campaign manager for Michael Basch, a techno-optimistic Democratic NYC mayoral candidate, a gig he secured by asking the only person he knew in politics to introduce them. He’s also worked as a consultant for NBA Africa and managed downtown restaurants like Regina’s Grocery and Miss Lily’s. The Bench is one of four Bengio ventures; he also co-founded the supper club Shtick with his wife, Jacqueline Lobel, and partners with the Hancock Foundation and the Hancock Cafe. On any given event night, he can be found buzzing around the room, excitedly facilitating introductions for his guests.
The son of a Moroccan father and Algerian mother, Bengio grew up in Strasbourg, France. When I ask what motivated him to move to New York in 2001, he deadpans: “Ever heard of the American dream?” More specifically, though, he was jealous of a friend who moved to the States for six months and returned speaking fluent English. “He was the coolest kid,” Bengio says. “And I was like, ‘I want to go to America, too.’ I love basketball,” he says, reorganizing a pile of books so that the edges aligned just so.
Bengio, a first-time voter, is coy about his own politics. Instead, he’s driven by the promise of America “that you can coexist,” he says, and a desire to nurture civil, democratic debate. “I want to be part of the project.”
“We need to really recommit and reaffirm what we mean when we talk about free speech—expression that is unencumbered by political interference in any way, shape, or form,” says Josef Palermo, a former curator at the Kennedy Center who drove up from the nation’s capital to attend this party. Earlier this year, Palermo wrote about the politicization of the Kennedy Center by both the Biden and Trump administrations in an article for The Atlantic. “We need spaces like this in D.C. Everybody’s in their own camps and certain venues are definitely coded one way or the other. I think having something like this would be huge in our nation’s capital.”
Then again, it’s partly New York’s distance from the D.C. swamp that makes talking about politics at The Bench feel cool. The space is decorated with Bengio’s enviable collection of NBA and political memorabilia. (He jokes that he stays up late scrolling vintage sites and bidding on Americana rarities.) Alongside Michael Jordan Wheaties boxes and a slew of rare basketball sneakers, there’s a framed copy of Emile Zola’s 1897 letter to the French youth during the Dreyfus affair, a portable Florida voting booth from the Bush vs. Gore election, a framed paper shift dress from Richard Nixon’s 1968 presidential campaign, and nearly every issue of John F. Kennedy Jr’s George magazine. The one with a Donald Trump cover gets taken down from the wall often, Bengio says, but he always puts it back up.
On Tuesday night, there appeared to be other collectors of rare political merch. Vintage Obama-era crop tops caught my eye, and a speechwriter for a New York City council member waxed poetic about his favorite vinyl record: a collection of John F. Kennedy speeches. Two guys wore t-shirts they designed themselves that cheekily quoted Michigan turncoat Haley Stevens: “Israel cums to me in my dreams.” (One of them requested anonymity, fearful of being cancelled by the Canary Mission, an anonymous organization that tracks critics of Israel.)
A good number of attendees who were professionally invested in the election outcomes couldn’t stop checking their phones. Anthony DiMieri, the man behind Mamdani’s winning social media strategy, told me he’d just come from Brad Lander’s party. Max Altman, the brother of the OpenAI founder Sam, also stopped by. He’s excited about a recent move to New York from Austin, Texas, and if he hadn’t forgotten to request an absentee ballot, he says, he would’ve voted for James Talarico.
As the results turned progressively blue, the room began to clear out. Before leaving, I chatted with Azoulay’s “libertarian friend” Hunt Beaty. In the hallway between broadcasts, Beaty tells me he’s not terribly moved by the midterms. “Everything interesting that is happening in the world right now, to me, is happening outside of politics,” he says. He rejects the libertarian designation and lives by the credo “free minds and free markets,” citing Reason magazine. And yet, Beaty finds that The Bench still has something to offer him.
“It’s fun to be in a room filled with buzzy, interesting people who at least are able to try and talk about ideas, while also being like, ‘Maybe we’re doing coke in the bathroom, too.’ I want there to be a New York City where those things could coexist.”
news.summary: At The Bench, a Lower Manhattan hub for self-described political outsiders, scenesters of various political persuasions took in the congressional blue wave together.
news.author: Jonah Rosenberg,Savannah Sobrevilla

news.title: Gov. Gavin Newsom commutes over 500 death sentences in California
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to commute all 548 state death row sentences to life in prison without parole before leaving office. 

Newsom stated that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California values, while acknowledging the decision will cause pain for victims' families. 

Under the California constitution, state Supreme Court approval is required to grant clemency to individuals convicted of multiple felonies. 

The American Civil Liberties Union praised the commutations as a necessary end to an error-prone and inhumane punishment. 

Newsom, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, previously noted he would not run if Kamala Harris enters the race.
news.author: Brittney Donovan

news.title: Gavin Newsom says death penalty is 'incompatible' with California values in massive commutation announcement
news.text:
Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will commute the sentences for all California prisoners on death row.

The historic decision will be one of the last of his administration since he has been term-limited out of office.

'Faithfulness to our values is measured by how we act when it is most difficult to uphold them. For me, this is one of those instances.'

Newsom cited moral reasons for the decision in a lengthy statement Thursday.

"I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom said in the statement. 

"This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims' families," he added.

Newsom waited until after Election Day to make the announcement. Governor-elect Xavier Becerra (D) won the election easily against Republican Steve Hilton.

There are currently 548 people on death row in California, making it the largest death-row population in the Western Hemisphere, according to Newsom. They will now have a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. 

The state has also not executed anyone for two decades.

"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims," Newsom continued. "Faithfulness to our values is measured by how we act when it is most difficult to uphold them. For me, this is one of those instances."

RELATED: Gavin Newsom RAGES in expletive-ridden rant against Joe Rogan: 'Well done, tough guy!'

Newsom has hinted that he is exploring a run for president in 2028, but he has said he will back off if Kamala Harris mounts another run for president.

"I wouldn't do that to her. I wouldn't do that to you. I wouldn't waste everyone's time," Newsom said to CNN's Jake Tapper as they both tried to fly-fish. "Who needs that?"

news.title: India-born Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayoral race, defeats Karen Bass
news.text: India-born Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in a stunning upset, marking a major political shift in the United States' second-largest city.Raman, 45, who was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, defeated Bass after campaigning on promises to improve public services, tackle homelessness and reform policing. Her victory also reflects a growing challenge to established Democratic leaders from progressive candidates across the country.Raman's victory comes a year after democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani won the New York mayoral election. However, unlike Mamdani, Raman attracted relatively little national attention during her campaign and sought to position herself as an independent-minded progressive willing to break with her party on certain issues.Her entry into the mayoral race came as a surprise, particularly after she had initially endorsed Bass, who was once her political ally. Raman announced her candidacy shortly before the filing deadline, saying Los Angeles had reached a "breaking point".Bass conceded defeat and said she had called Raman to congratulate her."While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," Bass said in a statement, adding that she was committed to ensuring a smooth transition.Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a re-election bid. Her first term was significantly affected by the devastating Palisades Fire, which broke out while she was abroad and caught the city's fire department unprepared.The disaster destroyed homes and displaced residents, leaving many voters dissatisfied with Bass' handling of the crisis. The political fallout continued to haunt her campaign.RAMAN PROMISES CHANGERaman's campaign focused on addressing long-standing problems in Los Angeles, including homelessness, deteriorating public infrastructure and concerns over policing.She has promised to remove the city's police chief, whom she considers too accommodating towards federal immigration authorities. She has also pledged to improve basic civic services, including repairing pothole-ridden roads, damaged sidewalks and broken streetlights.On homelessness, Raman criticised Bass' approach as ineffective and proposed expanding medical outreach teams to work with people living on streets and in encampments. Her plan aims to build trust with homeless residents and eventually move them into permanent housing.She has also proposed creating more housing options to reduce the city's dependence on hotels rented to accommodate homeless people.Raman has said her measures could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when Los Angeles will host the Olympic Games. However, homelessness remains a persistent challenge in the region despite billions of dollars spent on tackling the crisis.Her campaign gained traction amid voter dissatisfaction with problems that continued during Bass' tenure. A Berkeley IGSLos Angeles Times poll conducted between October 19 and 25 found that around four in 10 likely voters considered reducing homeless encampments a top priority for the next mayor.POLITICAL ESTABLISHMENT BACKED BASSRaman's victory came despite strong support for Bass from prominent Democratic leaders, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.Nearly every member of the Los Angeles City Council also backed Bass, who previously served in the state Legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022.Billionaire developer Rick Caruso, who lost to Bass in the 2022 mayoral election, also said he was voting for the incumbent, although he stopped short of formally endorsing her.Raman, an urban planner, received backing from several advocacy and political organisations, including Our Revolution, founded by Senator Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. However, she had limited support from prominent local politicians.She also held a widely publicised private meeting with former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, signalling efforts to expand her political network beyond progressive circles.As mayor, Raman will face the challenge of governing a city of 3.8 million people that is grappling with homelessness, infrastructure problems and a struggling entertainment industry. Los Angeles is also home to a major port, leading universities and research institutions, and remains one of the world's major tourist destinations.- Ends

news.title: Rahm Emanuel knows how congressional Democrats can keep winning
news.text:
Democrats had a better night than anyone expected on Tuesday, winning sweeping majorities in both the House and the Senate as voters turned away from President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. Now, they have to figure out how to govern and contend with two more years of Trump’s presidency — and gear up to hold onto their new majorities in 2028.
It’s a familiar situation for the party: Two decades ago, voters unhappy with President George W. Bush and the Iraq War propelled Democrats to congressional majorities in the 2006 midterms. Two years later, President Barack Obama won his first term and Democrats won even more seats in the House and Senate.
Rahm Emanuel — a former US ambassador to Japan, Chicago mayor, White House chief of staff, and member of Congress — was there to witness it. He led the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2006 when it led the charge for a Democratic House majority, and helped steer that majority from 2007 to 2009 as Democratic caucus chair.
On Wednesday, he spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about how Democrats should think about their midterms success, what they should — and shouldn’t — do with their new power in 2027, and what all of that means for 2028.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
You’ve been here before personally, way back in 2006. It was a different Congress, a different president, certainly a different time. But can you tell people who don’t remember what position you were in back then?
In 2006, I was chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and led the effort to take back the House. Nancy Pelosi became speaker and I became caucus chair. I also helped in the 2008 cycle, where we added another 20 seats. So Democrats were in around 254 seats when President Obama put his left hand on the Bible.
And to put a finer point on it, George W. Bush is president in 2006. You guys win control of the House and Senate, and then use that control to notch another win in 2008. What did you do? What was the play?
Let’s pull back a little, take a wider lens. One, this is a repudiation of the Republicans, not a vindication of the Democrats. I always thought that we were going to have a blue wave. This is a tsunami. These are Watergate numbers. But what we do in 2027 will determine whether we have won.
The voters voted for change, not a Democratic version of more of the same. You have a broad-based coalition where non-MAGA Republicans and independents are giving the Democrats a second look. Solidify this as a working coalition. Make the election transformational, not transactional. Power-wash all of Washington, all three branches. Ban stock trading, ban prediction market participation, mandatory blind trust, mandatory term limits and/or retirement age.
And then what I call the Jared Kushner rule. No foreign money while in government and no foreign money two years after. No Saudi and Qatari blind trust for you. Do the hearings, but produce a piece of legislation that acts on the hearings.
Second, everything’s going up in price. What hasn’t? The minimum wage. The last time it went up, Nancy Pelosi was speaker. Pass a minimum wage, $20 by 2030.
Third, repeal all these tariffs that are driving prices up. Everything I just told you, you’ll get bipartisan votes. And it puts Trump in a position: You sign it, we win; you veto it, we win.
There’s obviously this tension between “legislate” and “investigate” right now. Based on last night, people want “legislate.” But a lot of the base wants justice. They want [Defense Secretary Pete] Hegseth out.
They want their pound of flesh.
Tell me how you think Democrats should balance the two.
It’s not an either/or. You should do the investigations. Where is the Venezuela oil money? Where is Jared Kushner’s secret account with the Qatari money and the Saudi money? And what was he doing for them for that price?
I’m all for that, but that’s not change. That’s the predicate. I’m against impeachment because it’s one person and you won’t get it done. All three branches need cleaning, not just one man. What about his Cabinet? Clean it all up.
The job of the Democrats is to roll up your sleeves and get to work. Some Democrats may think that this is a vindication vote. I think it’s a repudiation vote and we will earn the victory in 2027 by producing change.
Earn that trust, solidify that winning coalition that went from Texas to Maine. Solidify it. And I think if you listened to [House Democratic leader] Hakeem Jeffries last night, if you listened to [Senate Democratic leader] Chuck Schumer, they understand that the test is about to come. It isn’t behind us, it’s in front of us.
Hakeem Jeffries feels a little unknowable sometimes. What do you think of him as speaker of the House?
Well, it’s unfair because I’m close to him.
So tell us what we don’t know about him.
Pretty much all our conversations first start with what? Checking in on each other’s families. Now, we rush through it so we get to politics, but he takes his family seriously and his role as a parent very seriously.
But now he’s very important to the country.
I respect him for that. He’s also very observant and serious about his faith because I’ve gotten a number of texts back, “I can’t talk, I’m in service.” So I said, “Put the phone down, listen to the sermon, you’re going to need it.”
The other thing is that he’s a consensus builder, but he does know what he wants to get done.
He’s a consensus builder in a time where the Democratic tent feels like it’s never been bigger. Karl Rove’s in the tent now. How do you manage that tent?
I used to say to Speaker Pelosi — when I was caucus chair and we were counting votes and trying to move X or Y — that Rep. Mo Udall used to have a great joke: “What is the difference between a cactus and a caucus? In a cactus, the pricks are on the outside.”
With the numbers Hakeem will have, nobody can hold him hostage. When you’re at 221, everybody’s a kingmaker and they’re going to sit there and hold you hostage. When you’re at 250, Hakeem has the liberty to say, “When you walk out of here, make sure the door doesn’t hit you.”
You told Democrats that they should go after Republicans in 2028. And there are people who hear you say that and they go, “Absolutely.” And there are people who hear you say that, they want to reach through their TV screens and choke you because they’re hearing this 2024 “Let’s go campaign with Liz Cheney” mindset that did not work.
This is not a hypothetical. Go tell Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton, who’s a former Republican. Neil Bush, who gave everybody a permission slip in Texas, said, “I’m voting for Talarico.”
That’s an opening. What Kamala Harris did — they ran around talking about democracy. I’m talking about people’s pocketbooks. Having helped Sen. Hamilton, having helped Nancy Lacore, the [admiral] who just won in Charleston, South Carolina. Those are people that built a winning coalition.
The fact is, to flip red to blue, you had to get Republican votes and independents. If you want to keep going and keep winning and solidifying this coalition, you have to know who was part of it. If you think you’re going to go into 2028 just on the backs of Democrats, God bless you. Swing voters in swing states swing presidential elections.
I’ll give you an example. This will get me yelled at. President [Joe] Biden made a pledge in 2020 to govern and bring America together. He spent a good portion of his presidency bringing the party together, not the nation. And I think it cost him politically.
Who do you like as a candidate in 2028? And you can’t pick yourself.
I’m not going to do that. I’m not going to answer that. Because here’s the good news for you. In 2024, let’s be honest, the party didn’t have a choice. We were told who our nominee is.
In 2028, you’re going to have Baskin-Robbins — 31 flavors. And if I decide to do this, you’re looking at Rocky Road.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Won His Senate Seat With a Mandate on Palestine. Can He Deliver?
news.text:
One senator out of the 100 who will fill the upper chamber of the 120th Congress was elected to his seat on a loud campaign promise to end U.S. complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza. 

Abdul El-Sayed will walk into a newfound Democratic majority after animating his base with pro-Palestine pledges seldom heard from a U.S. Senate contender. As a first-term senator, he’ll lack seniority on the committees to which he’s assigned. And although his critiques of the U.S. relationship with Israel have proven overwhelmingly popular in public opinion surveys and among voters at the polls, the same can’t be said for most of his soon-to-be colleagues.

“It’s going to be a fight,” said Beth Miller, political advocacy director for Jewish Voice for Peace Action, which supported El-Sayed’s campaign. “The Democratic establishment, when it’s in control, has not taken measures in support of Palestine in the past. And so this is about making sure that now they finally start listening to what the overwhelming majority of their bases say.”

El-Sayed’s run marked the first time the Jewish-led, anti-Zionist group backed a Senate campaign. Pro-Palestine lobbying groups like JVP Action have been pushing for legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel for years, aligning themselves with a small but growing number of left-leaning House members. The group helped author the Block the Bombs Act, introduced by Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., which netted 82 co-sponsors and became a pro-Palestine litmus test in some Democratic primary campaigns.

Building consensus around a single bill in the Senate is harder, but the upper chamber offers stronger levers to pull. Senators can force votes called Joint Resolutions of Disapproval that would block foreign security assistance, such as weapons sales to Israel. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has exercised this option repeatedly throughout the genocide in Gaza to try and block the sale of certain bombs, firearms, and other military equipment to Israel. While his resolutions failed in the Republican-controlled Senate, the most recent ones drew support from wide majorities of Democrats — soon to be the party in power.

Yet with the looming threat that Democrats might actually be able to pass legislation, El-Sayed would find himself under pressure from the likely Senate majority leader, Chuck Schumer, who has long maintained the support of the pro-Israel lobby, to fall in line with party priorities.

“The question is, ‘Who does he want to be?’ Does he want to be someone like Bernie, who is willing to sometimes stand up to leadership?” said Hamid Bendaas, communications director for the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which also backed El-Sayed’s run. “It’s hard to do that as a freshman and someone who’s just getting in there.”

Bendaas expressed confidence that the Michigan senator would be a champion of pro-Palestine legislation, but he noted that El-Sayed would have to balance his priorities, especially after running a campaign focused on economic populism and providing universal healthcare through Medicare for All. 

Shifting Winds

There is a tension revealed by the dilemma facing Sen.-elect El-Sayed: While a growing share of Americans — and an overwhelming majority of Democrats — disapprove of the U.S. spending billions of dollars on aid to Israel, voters’ clear No. 1 concern in the 2026 election cycle was the cost of living and their own economic precarity.

Some pundits have encouraged pro-Palestine candidates like El-Sayed to put their anti-genocide principles aside, arguing that more moderate Democrats performed better on Tuesday night. They compare El-Sayed’s 7-percentage-point defeat of Mike Rogers to James Talarico’s 12-point win over Ken Paxton in Texas — and some have already asked Talarico to defy his new colleague.

But on the campaign trail, El-Sayed often connected the issues of a high cost of living and outsized U.S. spending on aid to Israel. “We ought to be spending our money here, to build schools and provide healthcare and child care here, rather than sending our money abroad to a foreign government that’s done terrible things with our money,” he said in a September interview with Bloomberg TV. El-Sayed’s approach made him the target of nearly $40 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which supported widespread anti-Arab and Islamophobic attacks and accusations of antisemitism in an attempt to keep a vocal critic of Israel out of the Senate. 

“None of it mattered,” said Yousef Munayyer, a senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington D.C. who likened the gravity of El-Sayed’s win to that of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “And this is not the Commie Corridor. This is a swing state. A lot of taboos here have been shattered, and people are going to learn from this and be emboldened now.”

In addition to bringing joint resolutions to block future weapons transfers — like the Trump administration’s planned sale of $2.8 billion in 2,000-pound bombs to Israel — El-Sayed could introduce resolutions citing the Foreign Assistance Act; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., used one to demand a State Department report on Israeli detention of Palestinian children and Israeli military and settler killings of American citizens in the West Bank. He would also be able to introduce amendments to the Pentagon’s annual spending bill that carves out billions of dollars in joint U.S.–Israel weapons research. (The Senate is currently sitting on this year’s $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, which would even more deeply enmesh Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.)

Munayyer, the former head of the U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights, said that despite the uncertainty over whether moderate Democrats will be willing to link arms with progressives next session, El-Sayed’s win creates an environment ripe for accountability over Israel.

“You have a climate now where there’s going to be a lot less intimidation felt by people who had previously been hesitant to speak out on these issues because they thought it was political suicide,” he said. 

Even Republicans are beginning to feel the shifting winds. On the morning of Election Day, President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Fox News that the U.S. would halt the annual $4 billion in military aid to Israel. The move would only cut off one path for Israel to get weapons from the U.S. — still allowing direct weapons sales to Israel from U.S. companies and weapons development and sharing with the Pentagon — and Trump said it was made in agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who had been previewing it for months. Tactically, Trump said the goal was to take a “talking point” away from Democrats. He cited El-Sayed by name.

While ballots were still being counted on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance, an expected 2028 presidential contender, posted on X an early post-mortem of the massive GOP losses across the country. He wrote that the party could bring back “voters who had abandoned us” if they “End the war” in Iran and “Change our relationship to Israel.”

Such recognition from the Trump White House is new territory for U.S. politics, Munayyer said.

“We are about to witness, in my view, something we have never seen before in American politics,” Munayyer said. “A robust debate in the presidential primary campaigns in both parties, where the question of the U.S.-Israel relationship is going to come up time and again. That’s never happened before, and it’s gonna be seismic.”

The question is whether Democrats will stay on top of the wave. If Schumer, a staunch supporter of Israel, remains in charge of the Senate majority, he’ll have power over appointments to key committees — giving him the opportunity to curb the influence of a figure like El-Sayed. 

“I don’t think that Democrats want to have a messy fight about this stuff when the base is largely in agreement on it,” Munayyer said. But while Senate Democrats have evolved on the issue of Israel and Palestine — even Sanders expressed far weaker critiques of the Israeli state a few years ago — it’s one thing to be the dissenting party when you’re in the minority. It’s another to wield serious power.

Constant Pressure

El-Sayed is perhaps the most vocal supporter of Palestinian rights of any U.S. senator elected since James Abourezk of South Dakota, who in the late 1970s became the first Arab American to serve in the Senate. Abourezk frequently advocated for a Palestinian state and was an early critic of the pro-Israel lobby. After his time in Congress, he founded the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee. 

El-Sayed, now the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, frequently referred to Israel on the campaign trail as an “ethnostate” and said he opposes any nation that organizes its government by ethnicity and religion. In an appearance on ABC News, El-Sayed argued Israel was not a U.S. ally. Two days before the election, he spent a large portion of his sit-down with “60 Minutes” calling for Palestinians’ right of self-determination and repudiated the question of whether Israel had a right to exist. In his victory speech, he criticized attempts by pro-Israel critics to conflate advocacy for Palestinians rights as “hate.” 

Even so, in the lead-up to the general election, El-Sayed started being subjected to pressure from some on the pro-Palestine left. Critics chastised his decision to stump with former Vice President Kamala Harris over her complicity in the Biden administration’s support for the genocide in Gaza. Similar ire was directed at his partnership with former President Barack Obama, who has yet to name or condemn the genocide and governed over U.S. wars in the Middle East that saw the United States kill thousands of civilians.

Advocates for Palestinian rights, however, told The Intercept they recognized the utility in El-Sayed’s campaigning with the highest-profile members of the Democratic Party, and they counted it as a success that he earned their support. But they said they were not pinning all their hopes on a single individual. 

On top of all the other calcified interests and long-standing political biases that shape the U.S. Senate, there’s the influence of the sprawling U.S. weapons industry, with manufacturing giants like Lockheed Martin and Boeing lobbying for their interests and showering politicians in campaign cash. That industry wants to keep profiting off the genocide in Gaza, said JVP Action’s Miller, and El-Sayed alone is not enough to stop that.

“This is not gonna be that one man comes into the Senate and changes everything,” she said. “This is that one person has been elected with a mandate that has demonstrated where the masses of people are at on this issue, and now we have to keep fighting harder than ever before.”

news.title: Donald Trump Is Losing Young White Men Who Voted for Him
news.text:
The Republican Party has just suffered one of its worst defeats in my lifetime, on par with the 2006 "thumping" it endured in response to then-President George W. Bush's unpopular Iraq War. Having failed to internalize this lesson, the GOP proceeded to launch another unpopular war in the Middle East—this time not even bothering to consult the American people, international allies, or Congress—and it has come to the same end: an electoral bloodbath.

So what went wrong? The aforementioned war in Iran, first and foremost, is clearly the cause of much discontentment toward the Trump administration. The war has impacted energy prices, and voters are known to punish the president's party for overlooking basic economic reality. Widespread tariffs have also hurt the economy, and along with excessive immigration enforcement and the baseline level of corruption within the administration, it has probably looked to voters like President Donald Trump is indifferent to their hardships.

The GOP's diminished share of the young white male vote is particularly noteworthy. Much ink was spilled in 2024 over the Trump campaign's success at courting the podcast bro demographic, which is disproportionately young and male. (Not all of them are white—Trump actually performed remarkably well with black male voters under 25.) They share certain characteristics: skepticism of establishment media, disenchantment with both political parties, opposition to foreign military intervention, and hostility to wokeness, cancel culture, and scolding in general. Trump did an impressive job of reaching these voters and communicating that he was the guy who took them seriously. He understood their vibe; former Vice President "Momala" Kamala Harris did not.

Well, a lot can change in two years. Young white men shifted massively against Republicans, according to exit polls. This group swung 28 points toward Democrats; men overall swung 36 points. This means, contrary to the assumptions of many right-wing pundits, that the GOP's problem is not merely that non-white voters refuse to vote for them—since they actually lost their key demographic. Conservative commentators often argue against immigration on the grounds that diluting the white share of the vote is intrinsically harmful to their electoral prospects, but these midterms disproved that yet again because it wasn't just the non-white voters who picked the Dems.

Contra the "demographics is destiny" argument, men—even young white men in particular—shifted much harder than Latinos. Trump lost these voters on the economy, the war, and corruption.
The "podcast bros," whatever you think about them, were actually an early warning sign. pic.twitter.com/UIM3GqfhMl
— Christopher Rufo (@christopherrufo) November 4, 2026

"It turned out that reversing 'woke' culture and reclaiming traditional masculinity weren't enough for a demographic that was struggling to stay afloat in a difficult economy and strongly opposed Trump's unpopular war with Iran," writes Rosie Gray in The Washington Post.

She continues
news.summary: The administration has to think about doing something for this group beyond mere fan service.
news.author: Jason Russell,Robby Soave

news.title: Nithya Raman ousts incumbent Karen Bass in LA mayor's race, CBS News projects
news.text: Councilmember Nithya Raman will be Los Angeles' next mayor after defeating incumbent Karen Bass in the November general election, CBS News projects.Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day. Raman released a video statement on Thursday afternoon saying she is deeply honored to be the next mayor of LA. "Thank you to the thousands of people who knocked on doors, sent texts, made phone calls, convinced their neighbors to believe in the promise of this big, beautiful, joyful city that we get to call home," the video said. Raman spoke directly to people who voted for Bass or didn't vote at all, saying she is "going to City Hall to work every single day to earn your trust, and to earn your trust in this city again."In the video, Raman also paid tribute to Bass, thanking her for her decades of service and highlighting her as the first woman mayor of LA. "She has served Los Angeles for so many decades and I know so many people, not just across this city but across this country, are grateful for her dedication to the promise of Los Angeles," Raman said. Bass released a statement on Thursday morning conceding to Raman, saying she called her to congratulate her on the victory. "While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition," Bass wrote.Bass thanked her supporters and other leaders who helped during her campaign. She added that she will continue to "ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."Raman, a Democratic socialist, has been riding her momentum after pushing past Spencer Pratt in the June primary, but suffered a setback with voters a week before the election, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times.A survey released by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the LA Times shortly before the election showed Bass and Raman tied, with 40% support among likely voters.Bass and Raman became frontrunners after the primary election when they rallied ahead of third-place candidate Spencer Pratt. Councilmember Nithya RamanRaman announced her surprise bid for mayor in February after previously endorsing Bass' reelection bid.During the primary, Raman called her campaign a "long shot" before ultimately overtaking Spencer Pratt to face Bass in the general election.Before being elected to Los Angeles City Council in 2020, Raman served as the co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council Homelessness Committee and co-founded a homeless advocacy nonprofit.One of her most notable acts in office came in 2025, when she introduced a motion capping maximum annual rent increases for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments built before 1978. It eventually passed 13-2. She said she hoped to undertake similar work to help small businesses.Mayor Karen BassAfter serving more than two decades in public office as a congresswoman and as LA's 43rd Mayor, Bass said this race will be her last campaign for office. Bass was raised in LA with her three brothers. She began her professional career as a nurse and physician assistant, where she later founded the Community Coalition to help underserved residents of South LA battle substance abuse, poverty and crime.She kickstarted her career in politics in 2004 as a member of the California Assembly, where she became the first Black woman to serve as Speaker of a state legislative body. She left the Assembly in 2010 to run for Congress, where she served in the House for 12 years.Leading up to the primary election, Bass received endorsements from notable politicians including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Nearly a week before the November election, billionaire Rick Caruso threw his support behind his former rival in the 2022 mayoral race and vowed to vote for her in November."For the love of LA, I must put the past behind me because this election must be about our future," Caruso said in a post to X. "I will be casting my ballot for Mayor Karen Bass."He also said in the video that he had concerns about Raman that were not "much about ideology, but about competence."
news.summary: Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.
news.author: Chelsea Hylton,Matthew Rodriguez

news.title: ‘LA's Mamdani’ wins mayoral race as her Israel stance divides Jewish community
news.text: Just a week ago, the Democratic Socialists of America threatened to expel Nithya Raman from its ranks because she would not explicitly commit to a boycott of Israel. Now the 45-year-old Democrat is the mayor-elect of Los Angeles, America's second-largest city and home to one of the world's largest Jewish communities. NBC News projected Thursday that Raman had defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. Born in India and brought to the United States at age six, Raman previously accused Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza and operating an "apartheid state." Raman's victory marks another significant win for the American socialist left in an election that saw progressive forces gain strength across the country. According to the latest count, Raman received approximately 52.1% of the vote, compared with 47.9% for Bass, a margin of about 35,000 votes. Bass initially led on election night, but the picture shifted as counting progressed, partly reflecting support for Raman among younger voters, who were more likely to cast ballots on Election Day rather than vote early. Reacting to her victory Thursday evening, Raman said: "It is an enormous honor to be your next mayor." She paid tribute to Bass, saying her opponent had "dedicated decades of her life to the city." Bass conceded defeat, saying: "This is not the result we had hoped for, but the people of Los Angeles have spoken." She said she had called Raman to congratulate her and promised a smooth transition. In her statement, Bass also criticized President Donald Trump, accusing him of sending federal forces into Los Angeles "to spread fear and intimidation." It is the first time in 21 years that a sitting Los Angeles mayor has lost a reelection bid. The upset followed months in which Bass was considered particularly vulnerable, although polls in the final weeks of the campaign struggled to separate the two candidates. Bass, 73, a former congresswoman and the first Black woman to serve as Los Angeles mayor, entered the race with the backing of the Democratic establishment, including Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. Even all 14 of Raman's fellow City Council members endorsed Bass. But public patience had worn thin. The devastating wildfires of January 2025, which destroyed parts of Pacific Palisades and left hundreds of Jewish families among those who lost their homes, became a symbol of Bass' perceived failures. She was in Ghana on an official visit as part of a U.S. delegation attending the country's presidential inauguration and remained outside Los Angeles for more than 24 hours after the fires began. Her decision to travel despite earlier warnings about wildfire risks sparked public outrage, and she later acknowledged that the trip had been a mistake. The city's soaring housing costs, streets lined with homeless encampments and a growing perception that City Hall had lost control added to the frustration. Criticism also accumulated within the Jewish community over Bass' response to pro-Palestinian demonstrations and violent confrontations at UCLA and outside the Adas Torah synagogue in the Pico-Robertson neighborhood, where police subsequently acknowledged that they had not been adequately prepared. Raman seized on that discontent. In February, on the final day for filing candidacies, she announced a surprise challenge against Bass, whom she had previously supported. She promised to cut the number of people living on the streets in half by the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, accelerate housing construction and make the city more affordable for middle-class residents. She also pledged to remove Police Chief Jim McDonnell, partly over his department's handling of immigration enforcement raids by the Trump administration's Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. The police officers' union warned that her election could trigger a mass departure of officers and lead to "Armageddon" in the city. Raman was born in Kerala, India, and moved to the United States with her family at age six. She studied at Harvard and MIT, later returned to India to work with residents of impoverished neighborhoods and subsequently founded an organization helping homeless people in Los Angeles. In 2020, she unseated an incumbent City Council member, becoming the first woman of South Asian descent elected to the council. She lives in Silver Lake with her husband, a screenwriter who worked on the television comedies 30 Rock and Modern Family, and their twins. The nickname "LA's Mamdani" stuck because of Raman's affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America, the organization that also helped propel New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani to power. But her relationship with the organization has been considerably more complicated. In 2020, Raman said she did not support a boycott of Israel and warned against demonizing Israel and Jews. Following the October 7 Hamas massacre, she was among the first City Council members to condemn Hamas and criticized a DSA statement for what she said was its lack of empathy toward Israeli victims. Since then, however, her positions have changed. Jewish and Israeli communities in LA voice concern In an earlier interview with anti-Israel streamer Hasan Piker, Raman described Israel as an "apartheid state" and its war in Gaza as "genocide." At a September meeting with hundreds of Jewish voters, she repeated the genocide accusation and described the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, or BDS, as a "legitimate form of nonviolent protest," drawing negative reactions from attendees. Raman sought to explain that she recognized Israel's right to exist and had no intention of promoting a boycott through City Hall, but many in the audience remained unconvinced. Bass, who appeared at the same forum, rejected the genocide accusations and pledged to oppose a municipal boycott. Raman's position also placed her at odds with parts of the socialist movement. The Democratic Socialists of America's national leadership considered withdrawing its endorsement because she would not explicitly commit to supporting a boycott of Israel, creating an unusual confrontation between the organization and one of its most prominent electoral candidates. The election result was received with concern among Israelis and Jews in Los Angeles. "Voters in the city now have the pleasure of choosing between the complete incompetence of Mayor Bass and the political radicalism of her challenger, Raman. Good luck to all of us," a Jewish Beverly Hills resident told ynet on the eve of the election. Jewish community leaders have not spoken with one voice. Rabbi Noah Farkas, president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, said Raman's remarks about Israel had damaged the trust of many community members. Nevertheless, he made clear that the federation intends to work with the incoming mayor and demand that she protect Jewish and Israeli residents. Liberal Jewish community organizations, meanwhile, expressed confidence in Raman. They pointed to her visits to synagogues on Shabbat and Yom Kippur and her efforts to promote community safety. For many Jewish residents, her first major test will be whether she can protect religious institutions and effectively confront antisemitism in the city.
news.summary: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman defeats Karen Bass 52.1% to 47.9% after a campaign marked by disputes over Israel and boycotts; Jewish leaders say her genocide accusation damaged trust but pledge to work with her on combating antisemitism
news.author: Daniel Edelson, New York

news.title: G2 Esports Parts Ways With Head Coach Luka 'Perkz' Perković After His 'Tweet Bomb' Sparks Backlash
news.text:
G2 Esports has parted ways with its head coach and retired League of Legends player Luka "Perkz" Perković following divisive comments he made in a lengthy post on Twitter/X.

The 2,676-word-long tweet was published on November 4, 2026. Perković described it as his “first and last honest post in [the] last decade,” where he could “address some things honestly.” He explained that he’d written the statement to clarify his stance on certain topics “so that, at the very least, you can hate me for what I really stand for, and then that's completely fine by me.”

In the post, which he jokingly called a “tweet bomb,” Perković said he is not a fan of and does not endorse the Tate brothers in any way; claimed that “doesn’t really do politics” and has never “ever voted once” in his life; said he is not a fan of either Donald Trump or Kamala Harris; said he is a devout Catholic; denied being a “Putin fanboy” or being on the side of Russia in the war on Ukraine; and shared his stance on abortion, comparing it to “murder.”

“I don’t really do politics, nor have I even ever voted once in my life. I do have opinions, and I wish I was more educated on the topic, but the truth is I’m not, so I stay away from it,” he wrote. “There are some things I stand for, very simple things in life, but the only thing that is unshakeable for me, how it’s so widely accepted in public, is abortion. I cannot comprehend how people do not understand that is a muder, as life is created at conception. That is one view I will die by and never change.”

Perković also addressed his relationship with retired League of Legends pro and former G2 CEO Carlos "ocelote" Rodríguez Santiago, who stepped down from the company in 2022 after sharing a video of himself at a party with Andrew Tate. “Me standing up for Carlos publicly when he was being cancelled has nothing to [do] with all the things I’m all accused of supporting. Trafficking? Misogyny? Nazism? War? Are you okay?” Perković said of the matter.

“Carlos believed in me when nobody else did. I did not have a close relationship with my family when I was 16, including my parents, [who] I was not too close with, either. …Carlos and I have gone both completely different ways. He is his own person and I’m completely my own. In the end Carlos’ ego is something that put an end to his esports career, which was f**king insane. So there is a lesson to be learned in there, as well. We have a lot of different views on life.”

Perhaps the biggest takeaway from Perković’s post was his stance on abortion. This particular remark was a main talking point among fans and fellow players on social media, sparking a massive wave of backlash against him. G2 Esports addressed the situation in a public post mere hours later, where they confirmed that they have parted ways with Perković due to his tweet.

Their full statement is as follows:

“Last night, like many of you, we saw the statement shared by the Head Coach of one of our teams. G2 is a diverse and international organization with different people from all around the world. While the world is complex and not everyone agrees on everything, some of the statements made last night do not align with G2's stance and values. We have fans with different cultures and personal opinions, and it is of the utmost importance to us as an organisation that we respect and uphold this diversity when representing G2. We acknowledge that this statement hurt many of our fans, and we want to apologize for it.

“As a result, we have decided to terminate our collaboration with the individual. We will now focus on rebuilding our staff and roster for the next season and ask for your patience, as we will not be able to communicate any changes until free agency officially opens. - Alban Dechelotte, CEO of G2.”

Perković has since published one other tweet — a Bible verse from Luke 6:22. “Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man’s sake,” he wrote. This post, too, has received backlash from users. Perković has not posted anything else on his account at the time of writing.
news.summary: G2 Esports has parted ways with its head coach, Luka "Perkz" Perković, following divisive comments he made in a lengthy post on Twitter/X.

news.title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting block than some other Democratic candidates
news.text:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections. 

As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals, as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.

Wayne County voters

The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black. 

After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide. 

About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results. Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms, up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.

In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes, which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County. 

Statewide support is holding steady

In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3%, from 50.6% in 2020, as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris. 

Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote. 

In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.

Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.

Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024. 

While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll.

Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed. NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson, who won the governorship over Republican John James. 

Historic power and unity

Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement. 

Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate. 

However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity. Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates. 

Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination. If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.

My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations. 

An agenda that matters

El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program, while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education.

El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience. El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries. 

Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026. 

Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election. Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day. 

“I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.
news.summary: About 86% of Black Michiganders voted for Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate, according to preliminary data.

news.title: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman set to be next mayor of Los Angeles
news.text:
Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation’s second-largest city.

The India-born Raman’s upstart campaign marked a generational shift at City Hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign.

Her entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, once her ally. She said the city had reached a “breaking point” and announced her own candidacy just hours before the filing deadline, setting in motion a meteoric rise that would lead her to the mayorality.

In a video with the downtown skyline behind her, Raman paid tribute to Bass and thanked her volunteers. She promised to “build housing that people can afford, parks for our children to play in, a transit system that can get people where they need to go, a city that is safe for its working people and its families, and a city government that is actually capable of delivering on its promises.”

Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.

“While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said. “I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”

Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for reelection. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.

As votes were being counted earlier this week, Raman delivered an election night speech Tuesday that marked a campaign coda, summing up voters’ frustration with a city that seemed to be adrift, and her vision for the future.

“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she said. “LA stopped being a place where we could build things, where we could open things, where we could film things, where we could create things.”

She said she would restore “that ambitious Los Angeles, that joyful Los Angeles, that creative Los Angeles, that entrepreneurial Los Angeles.”

Raman’s rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.

Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities. She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years and left neighborhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights.

Raman called Bass’ efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She’s promising a new approach on the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors. Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless.

She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region.

Raman, 45, was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under the 73-year-old Bass. A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about 4 in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about 3 in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.

She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was “not ready for primetime” and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.

“Our city is in crisis,” she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicenter of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. “Where is our mayor?” Raman asked.

Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman’s views on policing and homelessness as “extreme.”

Raman’s victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the City Council. Bass served in the state Legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former President Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020.

In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.

Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians.

She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle. Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that’s home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions and serves as a major tourist destination.
news.summary: Nithya Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at City Hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year.

news.title: How Latino voters influenced elections with largest midterm turnout ever
news.text:
SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- Millions of Latino voters helped shape the outcome of key midterm races across the country, influencing some of the nation's most competitive congressional contests and contributing to what is expected to be the largest Congressional Hispanic Caucus in history.

Experts said the economy, including high gas and grocery prices, as well as immigration enforcement and deportation policies, were among the issues that drove Latino voters to the polls.

"This will undoubtedly be the largest turnout of Latino voters ever in a Midterm election," said Janet Murguía, president and CEO of UnidosUS.

MORE: Xavier Becerra projected to win California governor's race

Latino voters helped shape Tuesday's midterm elections, influencing races nationwide. The elections also resulted in California and Texas, the nation's two largest states, being led by Latino governors.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra defeated Republican Steve Hilton to replace termed-out Gov. Gavin Newsom.

In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Hinojosa became the state's first Latina governor and the first Democrat elected to the office in more than 30 years.

Christian Arana of the Latino Community Foundation said Latino voters were motivated by issues affecting their daily lives.

"We showed up, and we made it very clear that we are upset about the economy. We're upset about how our immigration policies are treating our community," Arana said.

MORE: Repudiation of Trump, economic pain drove Democrats to victory in the House: Voter Poll analysis

Political analyst and author Mike Madrid said Latino voters remain one of the nation's most influential voting blocs because they are less tied to major political parties.

"We are really the last true swing voters in American politics," Madrid said.

Madrid said Latino voters are more likely to identify as independent and less likely to align strongly with either major party.

"We again, are the most likely to be independent. We are the least partisan, and for better or for worse, we have an equal distaste for the political parties. There is no love lost for the Democrat or Republican party," Madrid said.

Analysts said that dynamic could make Latino voters even more important in the next presidential election.

"We are the truest swing vote out there in this country. And so if I'm someone looking to run for president this morning, I would call my advisors and ask them, what am I going to do to win over the Latino vote this coming 2028," Arana said.

UC Berkeley professor Lisa García Bedolla said voter turnout among Latinos is often a key part of the political story, noting that Latino voters turned out for this election.

"It's important to note that who stays home among Latino voters is always an important part of the story, because such a large proportion of Latino eligible voters tend to stay home, particularly during midterm elections," Bedolla said.

She pointed to the 2022 election and added: "It's not to say that there wasn't resonance from Candidate Trump in the Latino community in terms of his messages in 2024. There definitely was, but it was also a matter of the fact that the Democratic-leaning Latinos, particularly the ones that might have supported Kamala Harris, chose not to vote or weren't excited about voting. And so they had just as important an impact on the outcome as the ones who voted."
news.summary: A record number of Latino voters in a midterm election helped shape the outcome of key races across the country, including the election of Latino governors in the nation's two largest states, California and Texas.
news.author: Gloria Rodríguez,KGO

 By NIKKI SCHWAB, CHIEF CAMPAIGN CORRESPONDENT
