After President Donald Trump won a majority of Latinos in Texas in 2024, Democrats were despondent that the long-predicted blue wave in the Lone Star state would never come.
But after James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa scored smashing victories for Democrats, it's Republicans reacting with despair. 
Latinos in the state dramatically shifted leftward, with polling and anecdotes shared on the campaign trail with the Daily Mail suggesting it was prompted by economic anxieties and the Trump administration's overzealous immigration enforcement. 
Those working for Talarico's rival, Attorney General Ken Paxton, were in shock.
One adviser to a Paxton-aligned super PAC simply texted 'no,' when asked if they had anticipated the Latino vote running away. 
The collapse was stark along the border. In Starr County, which is 97 percent Latino and which Trump flipped by 16 points in 2024, Talarico won by an astounding 56 points. He left Ken Paxton in the dust, 77 to 21 percent. 
'It wipes out 10 years of work,' Austin-based GOP communications consultant Matt Mackowiak told the Daily Mail. 'It was clearly a reaction to overreach on ICE raids,' he said Wednesday.
'The only question is whether that loss of Hispanic support is temporary or not,' observed Mackowiak, who worked as a press secretary for Senators Kay Bailey Hutchison and John Cornyn, the outgoing GOP senator whom Talarico will replace. 

Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico (fourth from left) and gubernatorial hopeful Gina Hinojosa (fifth from left) stand onstage alongside Los Tigres Del Norte at a late October rally in Weslaco, Texas

Overall, Talarico beat Paxton 55 percent to 43 percent with 99 percent of the vote reporting. Latinos made up 24 percent of the electorate and 70 percent went for Talarico, while 29 percent selected Paxton, according to The New York Times. 
In the 2024 election, Trump won 55 percent of Latino voters in Texas statewide.
The president also flipped traditionally Democratic Rio Grande Valley border counties like Starr County, which gave him 58 percent of the vote, while Democratic nominee, Vice President Kamala Harris, had 42 percent. 
Governor-elect Hinojosa, who is from the Valley, defeated Greg Abbott by 42 points there. She carried Starr by 49 points. 
Voter registration in border counties rose 8 percent from 2022, the Texas Tribune found, the largest bump of any region in the state.
And Talarico won nine of the border counties Trump carried two years ago. 
The Democrats also gained a House seat in the Rio Grande Valley, with voters choosing Tejano musician Bobby Pulido over incumbent Republican Monica De La Cruz.
GOP redistricting efforts backfired too, with Democratic Representatives Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez retaining their seats despite the Republicans drawing them more red. 
On Fox News on Wednesday, Talarico credited his gains in the Latino community with showing up.

'I went down there a lot. I showed up, which is something a - a lot of national Democrats stopped doing,' Talarico replied. 'We took the Latino vote for granted.' 
'We took South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley for granted. And I refused to make that same mistake,' he said. 
Talarico said that Latinos were motivated by a mix of economic issues and immigration. They were upset with the Biden administration over border failures, he conceded, but added they were also alarmed by 'masked men in unmarked vehicles kidnapping people off our streets.'
Groups like Voto Latino also aided the Democrats on the ground, registering 412,000 Latino voters in Texas since the 2024 race. 
'For two years, we were told the Rio Grande Valley had shifted to the right, but at Voto Latino, we never believed it, and we were not going to take a chance,' Voto Latino President and Co-Founder María Teresa Kumar told the Daily Mail in an email. 
Ten days before the election, the group held a rally that featured both Talarico and Hinojosa. 
They also brought the iconic Mexican band, Los Tigres del Norte, into the fold. 
Kumar said their presence 'meant so much.' 
'They have sung the story of our community for generations, and when they took the stage, people felt seen. They felt heard,' she explained. 
With 95 percent of the vote counted, Talarico took Hidalgo County - which is 92 percent Latino and where Trump received 51 percent of the vote - with 73 percent to Paxton's 26 percent. 
Hinojosa won 71 percent to Abbott's 29 percent.
'Neither party gets to cash in on our community, and the Valley made sure of it,' Kumar said.

news.title: Scott Ritter: Buyer’s remorse made Trump. It has now also wrecked the Republicans
news.text:
American voters brought Donald Trump to power, handing him the opportunity to radically transform the political landscape of America, building upon overwhelming discontent about the political status quo that had metastasized over the course of successive presidential administrations, both Republican and Democratic.

And on November 3 American voters, in a fit of buyer’s remorse, voted for the very party they had rejected two years prior.

In 2024, Donald Trump was elected to a second term as president after running on a platform centered on the concept of “Making America Great Again,” or MAGA.

Riding on Trump’s MAGA coattails, Republicans were able to win control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, providing him with the opportunity to enact the kind of transformative changes in American politics his supporters were expecting – indeed, demanding. Two years later, the MAGA political machine lies in ruins.

Democrats, building on a wave of discontent and disappointment among an American electorate over the two-year track record of non-performance by Trump and his Congressional Republicans, have won decisive majorities in both houses of Congress, and are positioned to challenge Trump’s agenda for the remaining two years of his term.

news.title: The Blue Tsunami Was the Revenge of the Black South
news.text:
Voters in the 2026 midterm elections issued a stunning rebuke of the Republican Party on Tuesday, delivering Democrats control of both the House and the Senate, in addition to a majority of state legislative chambers, governorships, attorney general offices, and more. A Democratic victory of this magnitude—which turned even staunchly red states like Texas blue—hasn’t been seen in generations. And a new memo circulated among top Democratic National Committee officials on Wednesday acknowledges that voters of color were “the driving force” of this massive win.

The feat is all the more astounding because the voters of color who powered Democrats’ success were set up to fail. In July 2025, Donald Trump’s Justice Department started pressuring Texas officials to break up electoral districts where Black and Latino residents made up a majority of eligible voters. In August, Trump declared that Republicans were “entitled” to five more congressional seats and called on the state to redraw district maps to hand the GOP a structural advantage.

Texas, led by Gov. Greg Abbott (who just lost his reelection campaign) and Attorney General Ken Paxton (who just lost his campaign for Senate), did as it was told. And at Trump’s urging, several more Republican-led states soon redrew their district maps, aiming to maximize partisan gains at the expense of meaningful representation for voters. Experts predicted a precipitous drop-off of people of color in elected office, and warned that 20 of the Congressional Black Caucus’ 62 members could lose their seats.

Then, in April 2026, the Supreme Court poured fuel on the fire by eviscerating the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais. Justice Samuel Alito wrote for the Republican majority that district maps violate the VRA only if there is an “objective likelihood” of “intentional racial discrimination.” He stressed that maps drawn to achieve partisan goals easily pass that test, “even if it so happens that the most loyal Democrats happen to be Black Democrats.” And he emphasized that restoring the political power of people of color targeted with gerrymanders is unlawful, because that too is “intentional race-based conduct.” In other words, Alito gave Republicans the go-ahead to deny Black people an equal opportunity to participate in the political process.

Many advocates feared the worst: Between the 2024 and 2026 elections, Republican-led states reassigned over 25 million people, or roughly 7.5 percent of all Americans, into different congressional districts. One report concluded that “the only realistic path” for Democrats to avoid decades of Republican rule—and for Black voters to have any shot at electing candidates who represent their interests—would be “a rare ‘blue wave’ election scenario” where “voters turn out at overwhelming rates.”

Tuesday was not just a wave. It was a tsunami. Preliminary data from the University of Florida Election Lab indicates that approximately 48.8 percent of eligible voters participated in the 2026 midterm election, making it the second-highest midterm turnout in over a century. Other early reports indicate that Black voter turnout in particular soared, rivaling the numbers of Barack Obama’s first presidential run.

And Black folks are mad as hell: In a poll of 700 Black women shortly before the election, for example, 87 percent said that the nullification of the Voting Rights Act and the surge of racially discriminatory attacks on the franchise made them more motivated to vote. A New York Times analysis of 2026 midterm trends shows that 91 percent of Black voters supported Democrats—a considerably higher amount than that of any other racial group.

Republican elites underestimated Black voter turnout and overestimated their own level of support. Now, instead of collapsing, Black representation is expected to remain relatively steady in Congress. Black candidates made historic inroads in statewide elections for offices like the Senate, which are not affected by redrawing individual district maps; and in the House, Black candidates won many contested seats, gerrymandering be damned.

With Tuesday’s election of Juliana Stratton, for example, there will be three Black women concurrently serving in the Senate. For reference, Kamala Harris was only the second Black woman ever to be elected to the Senate, and between 2017 and 2021, she was the only one serving. As more ballots are tallied, Mississippi also appears on the cusp of sending a Black Democrat, Scott Colom, to the Senate. The last Black man Mississippi elected to the Senate was born into slavery in 1841.

In Louisiana, the state that fought for racial gerrymandering in Callais, Republican lawmakers responded to the Supreme Court’s decision by eliminating one of the state’s two majority-Black districts in order to send five Republicans to the House of Representatives. They may send only three: Rep. Troy Carter, a Black Democrat, handily held his seat in the sole remaining majority-Black district. And in two other districts, Black women Democratic candidates are maintaining narrow leads and advancing to runoff elections next month.

Alabama imposed a new map after Callais too, intending to dilute the Black vote and oust Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat. Figures won reelection by 8 points. Overall, Republicans are expected to pick up, at most, three of the 15 seats they targeted in Trump and Alito’s redistricting scheme.

Although the 2026 midterm election results are incredible, Americans should not be fooled into thinking Callais wasn’t so bad after all. Yes, as per usual, Black people pulled off something extraordinary. But also as per usual, we shouldn’t have to. Democracy can’t survive if it depends on persistently overcoming enormous racist obstacles. The good news is: Black voters gave Congress the numbers it needs to curb the power of the court and protect the power of the people.
news.summary: The Supreme Court tried to disenfranchise Black voters. Boy, did they have other ideas.

news.title: Newsom commutes all 548 death sentences in California as he prepares to leave office
news.text:
Gov. Gavin Newsom has moved to clear death row in California before he leaves office.

He announced on Thursday that he plans to commute every death sentence to life in prison without parole in a decision affecting 548 inmates who are currently on death row in the state.

The move comes as Newsom, who is known for feuding with Donald Trump, prepares to conclude his eight-year tenure as governor. He enacted an execution moratorium in 2019 but hundreds of convicts remained condemned. 

"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom said in a letter.

Under the state constitution, approval from the California Supreme Court is required to grant clemency to anyone convicted of multiple felonies. California voters rejected a ballot measure in 2016 that would have repealed the death penalty in the state.

Newsom said the decision was among his hardest as governor and acknowledged that it will bring back painful memories for crime victims’ families.

"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," Newsom wrote.

The American Civil Liberties Union, which is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, applauded the announcement.

“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” said executive director Anthony Romero in a statement.

The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.

Newsom, the 40th governor of California, is known for mocking Trump online, including with X posts written in all caps and riddled with spelling mistakes in an open mockery of Trump.

He’s long been considered a 2028 hopeful and has dominated prediction markets for months, peaking at 40 percent likelihood of being Democrats’ presidential nominee.

However, some analysts say his chances have since steadily declined. 

Newsom said in September that he won’t run for president if former Vice President Kamala Harris runs a third time and that his children would have the final say on whether he takes on a 2028 presidential run. 

“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom said. “Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time.”

Asked to elaborate, Newsom said pitting two California Democrats against each other would force their shared base to choose between them, handing an advantage to the other candidates.

“Electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it — mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good,” Newsom said.

Newsom endorsed Harris when former President Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 presidential election.

He shares four children with his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom.

“I know what matters in life,” Newsom said. “I’ve got four kids. It’s the only thing that matters to me. They gotta be on board.”
news.summary: Gov. Newsom has long been considered a 2028 presidential hopeful

news.title: Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman ousts embattled Mayor Karen Bass
news.text: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation’s second-largest city.The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at City Hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign.Her entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, once her ally. She said the city had reached a “breaking point” and announced her own candidacy just before the filing deadline.Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.“While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said. “I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for reelection. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities. She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years and left neighborhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights.Raman called Bass’ efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She's promising a new approach on the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors. Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless.She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region.RELATED STORY | Keisha Lance Bottoms to become Georgia’s first Black governor, first woman governorRaman offered changeRaman, 45, was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under Bass, 73. A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about 4 in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about 3 in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was “not ready for primetime” and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.“Our city is in crisis,” she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicenter of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. “Where is our mayor?” Raman asked.Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman’s views on policing and homelessness as “extreme.”RELATED STORY | Xavier Becerra wins California gubernatorial race, making history as the state’s second Latino leaderTop Democrats lined up with BassRaman's victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the City Council. Bass served in the state Legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former President Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020.In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians.She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle. Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that's home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions and serves as a major tourist destination.
news.summary: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass in LA's mayoral race.

news.title: What the midterms mean for 2028
news.text:
Welcome to The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. Let’s get into it.
One big idea
Tuesday night, in a midterm election for the ages, Democrats notched sweeping victories across the country. They took back both chambers of Congress, and possibly broke the spirit of a Republican Party that has been firmly in President Donald Trump’s grip for the last decade.
Early race calls in Georgia and North Carolina. Finally ousting Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. Historic wins in Texas and Iowa. Surprise wins in Kansas, South Carolina, and (maybe) Mississippi?
This was a bloodbath. A tsunami, not a wave. And it was a vindication for pollsters who had been flagging signs of Republican underperformance all year.
Most importantly, it was the clearest message the American public could send to Trump’s administration: This president, his priorities, and his war of choice in Iran are out of step with public opinion. Trump wasn’t on the ballot, but he repeatedly told people to vote like he was. Americans accepted the challenge and largely retired the GOP candidates functioning as his proxy.
Thinking about our reporting on America, Actually, where we’ve been charting the path to America’s post-Trump future one episode at a time, here are five lessons I’m taking from the results. They apply to the coming legislative fights in Congress and to the 2028 presidential primary.
1. It really was a populist backlash
Throughout the year, candidates from James Talarico to Abdul El-Sayed said this election wasn’t about right versus left, but top versus bottom. The results bore that out.
For two years, Republicans and their allies claimed Trump’s 2024 coalition was a firm realignment, a fundamental break from Democrats by working-class voters. Fast-forward to this week: The New York Times’ voter analysis shows every big demographic moved toward Democrats, including men (17-point swing, Latino voters (28-point swing), and Asian voters (17-point swing).
Two things drove this. First, Trump flopped, breaking his promises to lower prices and avoid foreign conflicts, among other things. Second, Democrats refocused their message, especially after Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 mayoral win in New York City, on affordability and tangible economic concerns. That brought back voters they lost in 2024, and reinforced the multiracial coalition they needed to overcome Republican advantages: a GOP-leaning Senate map, heavily gerrymandered districts, and a massive spending edge driven by big donors.
None of it mattered.
2. Issues that won: Affordability, anti-corruption, anti-data centers
So how did Democrats drive the bottom-versus-top message? Universally, with affordability, and by highlighting the choices Republicans made to follow Trump into the political abyss. Tariffs were the original sin. The Iran war made things worse.
When we were at a Speedway in battleground state Pennsylvania, even Trump voters were frustrated with the price of gas. Everyone, and I mean everyone, could draw the line between the war in Iran and the cost at the pump. When Pennsylvania voters are talking about the Strait of Hormuz, that’s a problem. It’s also a clear sign the GOP plan to blame the 2026 economy on former President Joe Biden wasn’t working.
Here’s what one voter said: “I blame the president because he indicated to us he’s gonna drop all these costs. I know it can’t happen overnight, but when is it gonna happen?… It’s outrageous.”
Two other issues carried the populist mood:

Democrats across the country began hammering Trump on corruption earlier this year, and there’s real evidence the message was potent. We heard it in Virginia, and candidates like Jon Ossoff and Talarico made it their calling card. It wasn’t just that Trump was for sale. It was that he and his family were profiting from big business while things got more unaffordable for you.
Data centers
The third ingredient in this populist stew. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Senate candidate Annie Andrews in South Carolina, and House candidate Will Lawrence in Michigan made a data center moratorium central to their campaigns. All three won. Data center moratoriums went an astounding 43-1 when put directly in front of voters, a sign of just how unpopular the issue has become.
And like affordability and corruption, the data center message was never about just one thing. Voters were mad about the secretive process. Anxious about what artificial intelligence means for the future of work. And particularly enraged that big technology seemed to be profiting at their expense.
All of that came out at the polls.
3. Issues that lost: The GOP culture war
The GOP had a huge spending advantage this cycle, and so much of that money went into ads painting Democrats as extreme, particularly on social and cultural issues. “Talafreako” in Texas, who they portrayed as an effeminate vegan. The Hasan Piker obsession in Michigan and the openly anti-Muslim and bigoted ads and rhetoric there and in places like Minnesota as well. And repeated hammering of a tactic that worked for Trump in 2024: stoking panic about transgender rights or “biological males” in women’s sports.
It flopped in 2026, and there’s no way around it. The spending spree didn’t just fail to pan out; they seem to have lit their money on fire, given how roundly Americans rejected the pitch. To the electorate, the most offensive thing wasn’t progressive overreach or nonbinary pronouns. It was Trump’s attacks on diversity and inclusion, and his party’s refusal to align its priorities with those of everyday Americans.
The GOP also had a timing problem: They ran a 2024 playbook against a 2026 Democratic Party that was much better positioned to beat back the caricature of progressive zealots.
* Beau Bayh in Indiana and El-Sayed in Michigan made direct appeals to the “bro” vote with weightlifting videos.
* Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, both religious liberals, put faith at the center of their campaigns.
These weren’t coastal elites. They were tailored to the district and the state. They spoke to the everyday person, not the Ford Foundation. And in doing so, they wrote a playbook against GOP attacks.
4. Standout demographics: Latino and rural voters
Two groups stood out to me: Trump’s collapse with Latino voters, and Democratic gains with rural voters.
Latino voters
The numbers are staggering. The Times estimates Hispanic voters were D+39, a 28-point swing leftward from 2024. Results in Texas, Nevada, and Arizona, and even the tightness in Florida, show the impact of Trump’s collapse with the all-important swing demographic. As we reported this summer, two issues drove Latino voters away from Republicans: the administration’s credibility collapse on the economy, and a backlash to the interior push for deportations.
Here’s what Stephanie Valencia of Equis Research said: “It’s the economy, it’s the war, and it’s immigration. It’s those three things.”
Rural voters
When we covered the stakes in state legislature races, and specifically Democratic efforts to win trifectas (governor plus both chambers) in states like Wisconsin and Nevada, rural voters were front and center. 
Democrats pulled off the trifecta in Wisconsin: Gov.-elect David Crowley, plus a flipped Senate and Assembly, the first Democratic trifecta there in 16 years. By early tallies, they also won trifectas in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, and Nevada.
It reminds me of what Francesca Hong told me when we met her on her tour of rural Wisconsin a few months ago: The midterm stakes weren’t just federal but state-level. Democrats won both.
5. 2028 winners and losers
Caveats apply: We should pump the brakes on extrapolating too much from the 2026 midterms to the 2028 presidential primary. But I think there are some things we do know.
Winner: Non-Vance Republicans
If you’re Ron DeSantis, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, or another Republican with credentials in Trump’s orbit who has also kept some distance, last night’s result helps make your case. Trump dragged the party down in Texas, South Carolina, and Ohio, where he and Vance defended Vivek Ramaswamy’s deplorable ad featuring his opponent’s estranged mother.
Going forward, Vance has to walk a tough line between acknowledging the country’s Trump distaste and not angering the president he serves under. His initial reaction to the midterm losses was to blame the Iran war first and foremost, notably without saying whether it was the wrong decision by his boss. But he’s spent the last two years all in on Trump mimicry, even defending the ICE shootings in Minnesota earlier this year. Is that a winning message anywhere? I’m not so sure.
Winner: Fresh faces on the Democratic side
Whether moderate or progressive, Democrats embraced younger candidates with new messages and bold ideas that match the scope of voters’ problems. That’s bad news for candidates who represent a specter of the past, mainly former Vice President Kamala Harris, who has courted speculation about another run through a series of media interviews.
There is no way to read these results as a desire to relitigate the same fights of 2020 or 2024. It’s a call to write a new story entirely. 
One thing I’m hearing
In an election night full of surprises, perhaps the biggest of them all was in Mississippi, where Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom is poised to possibly win his race against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, with the two separated by just dozens of votes with thousands more left to count as of this writing. We reached out to Mississippi Today reporter Michael Goldberg, fresh off covering a press conference with Colom on Wednesday, to walk us through what happened. 
Mississippi barely seemed to be on the national radar until the final weeks. What signs did you see in your reporting that this result was possible?
Colom began to pick up steam rapidly as the election entered its closing weeks, drawing an infusion of resources from national Democrats and a brigade of Democratic stars filing into Mississippi for campaign events. But while the national attention ramped up in the election’s home stretch, Colom ran a tireless campaign from the beginning, crisscrossing the state for in-person events and trying to run a digitally savvy campaign that captured attention online. Also, former Democratic gubernatorial candidate Brandon Pressley came within 4 points of winning the 2023 governor’s race, and many local Democrats have been urging the national party to take Mississippi seriously ever since. 
How big a factor were the Callais decision and voting rights? How did those issues come up in your conversations with voters?
Colom campaigned with US Rep. Bennie Thompson, the lone Democrat and lone Black member of Mississippi’s congressional delegation, who would be a likely target of a future redistricting push by the Republican-controlled state legislature. Colom has called the Callais decision “a threat to our democracy” the country hasn’t seen in decades. This fall, voters packed public hearings on redistricting and expressed their anger and dismay. 
What is Scott Colom like on the campaign trail? What was most distinctive about his campaign compared with other Mississippi Democrats?
Colom campaigned hard. He traversed the state from end to end and, in the election’s homestretch, engaged in a near-nonstop media blitz aimed at galvanizing any voters tuned into traditional cable news shows or following the race on social media. In viral ads, he mocked Hyde-Smith for suggesting voters upset over the rising price of beef should “pick another protein” and riffed off the Oscar-winning movie Sinners, which is set in Mississippi.
On the ground, Colom mobilized the Democratic base through energetic rallies and appearances with high-profile national Democrats. He also tried to persuade skeptical Republicans. In one 24-hour span just over a week before Election Day, Colom roamed the line outside a Trump rally in northeast Mississippi, spoke to some of the president’s supporters, then headed to the other end of the state for a rally with former US Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. 
Mississippi is often overlooked in national politics because it’s considered so reliably Republican. What’s the biggest thing people outside the state misunderstand or don’t know?
Many this morning have argued that regardless of whether Colom wins narrowly or loses narrowly, his campaign showed that with investment from the national party and the right candidate, Mississippi Democrats have a fighting chance of winning statewide.

news.title: Defeated Republican Claims ‘Jesus Christ Could Have Run And Would Have Lost’ This Election
news.text:
CNN chief congressional correspondent Manu Raju shared a few quotes on Wednesday from defeated Republicans about why they think they lost their respective races in the midterm elections, with Anderson Cooper and Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) delivering quite the gem.

Lawler lost his reelection bid in New York’s 17th Congressional District to Democrat Cait Conley, with Raju pointing out that Lawler already had an uphill battle, considering he was “one of the three Republicans running in a district that Kamala Harris actually carried in 2024.”

Raju said Lawler told CNN he believes he “ran as good a campaign as he possibly could” but that “the bottom fell out.”

When Raju pressed him a bit more about his loss, Lawler gave a nine-word response that is quite the head-scratcher.

“He said, ‘Jesus Christ could have run and would have lost,’” Raju recalled to Cooper.

“Wow,” Cooper responded. “That’s quite the quote.”

It’s unclear if Jesus would be down to run as a MAGA Republican and support President Donald Trump’s policies, like Lawler. But the soon-to-be former congressman may have a point about voters’ sentiments toward the GOP’s current state, judging by the midterm results.

If Lawler’s town halls are any indication, most of his constituents were pretty frustrated with the congressman’s loyalty to the president.

While being booed at a town hall in his suburban New York swing district in February, Lawler scolded the crowd for raising concerns about issues like immigration and tariffs.

“Folks, if you want me to answer the question,” Lawler said. “Let the question be asked and then listen to the answer.”

The lawmaker exhibited even more extreme behavior during a congressional hearing in July.

Lawler, who was invited to the hearing to simply introduce a witness, took the opportunity to spout off politically charged anti-immigration rhetoric as Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) tried their best to shut it down. Despite being warned and reminded several times that he was there just to introduce a witness, chaos ensued and Lawler was eventually booted from the hearing.

Lawler told TMZ outside of the hearing, “Frankly, Jamie Raskin and Pramila Jayapal are fucking assholes. Their conduct in that hearing was disgraceful.”

news.title: Surprising potential candidates top new 2028 presidential primary poll
news.text:
Days before Democrats' historic midterm election victory, a new AtlasIntel poll showed surprising frontrunners for the 2028 presidential primaries.

The poll, released on Nov. 1, showed Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Secretary of State Marco Rubio leading hypothetical primaries for their respective parties.

According to the poll, Ossoff held a tight lead of less than a percentage point over Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg ranked third, with former Vice President Kamala Harris coming in fourth.

For Republicans, the picture was a bit clearer, with Rubio holding a commanding lead over Vice President JD Vance. The GOP primary could be a two-horse race, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Tucker Carlson and President Donald Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., all polling under five percentage points.

The AtlasIntel poll surveyed 3,566 respondents from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1 with a two percentage point margin of error.

Falling frontrunners

The latest AtlasIntel poll significantly differs from other 2028 primary polls.

In late October, a Harvard/HarrisX poll found Harris and Vance leading their respective primaries, with both holding comfortable leads.

Among Democrats, Harris led California Gov. Gavin Newsom by 14 percentage points. However, in the latest AtlasIntel poll, Harris came in a distant fourth with 12.6%, and Newsom only had 9%.

Also in the Harvard/HarrisX poll, Republicans ranked Vance 19 points ahead of Trump Jr. and Rubio, while in the AtlasIntel survey, the vice president trailed Rubio by 13 points.

Rumbles, but nothing else

As of now, despite the midterms being over, no one has officially declared their intention to run in 2028.

Throughout midterm season, potential 2028 candidates like Vance and Harris, among others, consistently said they were focused on the upcoming midterm elections, without disclosing any presidential ambitions.

Following the midterms, Doug Sosnik, a Democratic strategist, told Reuters that different ideological sides of the Democratic Party will look to claim victory ahead of 2028.

"All kinds of wings of the Democratic Party can find affirmation in the results last night," Sosnik said. "I don't think that anyone can, nor should they, try to contain the differences we have as a party."

Contributing: Reuters

news.title: Nate Silver Makes Bold Prediction About Trump Exit Scenario
news.text:
Polling analyst Nate Silver says he has a “weird intuition” that President Donald Trump might “quit” after the GOP’s midterm catastrophe. 

The election forecaster, who correctly called the blue wave that handed Democrats both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, made his prediction while explaining that “Republicans made a deal with the devil in Trump.” 

“I mean that in the sense of, like, you get your three Supreme Court justices, you get tax breaks for the wealthy, but you pay a lot of price for that, right? Because Trump has so sucked out the oxygen from anybody else in the Republican party,” he told his co-hosts on the Still Counting podcast. 

Turning to Vice President JD Vance’s political future, Silver pointed out that then-Vice President Kamala Harris’s failure to distance herself from then-President Joe Biden hurt her campaign in 2024.

Noting that it used to be more common for vice presidents and presidents to be “rivals,” he then declared, “I mean, that’s part of why I had just a weird intuition that maybe Trump will find some pretense... to quit, you know what I mean?”

“Because he could get very, very, very isolated, and that also could make him dangerous,” Silver continued, arguing that the lame-duck president has “no f---ing leverage” with Republicans. 

“He has lost the fear factor,” he added.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

Vance, 42, has already begun trying to distance himself from his boss, blaming Trump’s deeply unpopular war with Iran for the party’s historic losses in a striking statement on X. 

“To the people who are p---ed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview,” he wrote, sounding much like a candidate on the campaign trail.

But Silver named Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds when asked whom he would put on the Republican ticket to give the party its best chance in 2028.

Silver isn’t convinced the worst is necessarily behind the GOP.

“I know the ‘smart’ conventional wisdom is that midterms don’t predict future election results,” Silver wrote Wednesday in a post on X, which featured a graph comparing Trump and George W. Bush’s abysmal approval ratings at this point in their second terms. “But then I look at this. And 2006 is the only modern lame-duck term with a wave like this.”

Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in 2006, then suffered another major defeat two years later when Barack Obama beat John McCain in the 2008 presidential election.

news.title: This Is How Pelosi Ends: Not With a Bang But With a Weirdo

Retiring two-time former House Speaker Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) once bestrode national and California politics like a colossus, if a frequently tipsy one. This isn't an obit, political or otherwise, but before we get to today's big news, you have to feel it deep in your bones what a presence the San Francisco congresscritter once was.

A blessing from Pelosi could take a Bay Area Democrat without much talent or charisma — I'm looking at you, Adam Schiff and Chris Van Hollen — and give them a real place on the national stage.

Pelosi was also one of the most wickedly effective House Speakers in history. She knew how to count the votes and twist the arms, and she knew where all the bodies were buried. Hell, she probably helped dig some of the shallow graves.

And Another Thing: One exception was Kamala Harris. Pelosi blessed her opponent, Terence Hallinan, in the 2003 San Francisco district attorney race, but Harris prevailed thanks in no small part to patronage from Willie Brown. 

Mostly, Pelosi knew how to use the law to enrich herself. She entered Congress in 1987 with a net worth estimated at a little under $3 million, including stocks valued at $610,000 to $785,000. Her stock portfolio — managed by her husband and alleged rough trade fan, Paul — generated a return of about 16,930% during her four decades in the House, while the Dow returned roughly 2,300% over the same period.

It's good to be the queen. 

When she and Sen. Harry Reid (D-Nev.) were busy assembling Obamacare like a Frankenstein creature, I always pictured her with two cellphones at the ready. One phone had Reid and Barack Obama on speed dial, and on the other one, her stockbroker.

Pelosi really was that shameless — and why not? It isn't like she would ever be held to account. She simply wielded too much money and power to be stopped. Besides, she was looked on in Congress as a role model, not a felon.

My, how the might have fallen. Ish.

She served her last two terms as a backbencher, likely trying desperately behind the scenes trying to make something out of her hand-picked successor, House Minority Leader (and next Speaker) Hakeem Jeffries. 

Her last act, more or less, was trying to anoint San Francisco Board of Supervisors member Connie Chan as her successor representing California's 11th district in congress.

But oh dear God.

Chan conceded the race yesterday to fellow — if that's the word — Democrat Scott Weiner, a state senator best known for... 

...how do I put this?

As a former San Francisco resident, I can tell you that Weiner is the kind of guy you'd expect to see wearing minimalist black leather attire at some Castro St. pride parade, not walking the halls of Congress. And as a state legislator...

...well, he's perhaps best known for stuff like this:

Pelosi is at least nominally Catholic — no wonder she didn't want Weiner winning her seat.

But neither Pelosi's money nor influence were up to the task of saving San Francisco voters from themselves.

news.title: Josh Shapiro's 'iron is hot' for 2028 presidential run as landslide win in Pa. sets stage for national audition
news.text:
The Democratic tide that swept through Pennsylvania in Tuesday's midterms, giving the party a trifecta in state government for the first time in more than three decades, is widely expected to prime the path for Gov. Josh Shapiro to make a presidential run in 2028. 

Shapiro, who defeated Republican challenger Stacy Garrity by a margin of 22 percentage points on Tuesday, wasted little time setting the tone for his second term. With Democratic control secured in Harrisburg, the table is now set for Shapiro to build his case for the White House. 

"There's a whole bunch of things that Republicans have been blocking for years," Shapiro said early Wednesday in an appearance on "CBS Mornings." "I want to get that done in the first hundred days with our trifecta."

Shapiro's broad popularity and resounding electoral success in a battleground state may be his strongest selling points for the Democratic ticket in 2028. Ahead of the governor's victory address Tuesday night, Pennsylvania Democratic Party chair Eugene DePasquale underscored the state's importance to the presidential race and boasted about gains in Democratic voter registration. The state has voted for the winner in the past five presidential elections. George W. Bush was the last president to get elected without carrying Pennsylvania.

"There is no math for a Democrat to win the White House without Pennsylvania," DePasquale said in Harrisburg. 

Shapiro, who was on Kamala Harris' short list for the vice presidential nomination in 2024, has avoided making public commitments on whether he'll run in 2028. He launched a federal political action committee in October to boost contributions to four Democrats who swept the state's competitive U.S. House races on Tuesday. The results showcased the impact of Shapiro's fundraising abilities at the national level, where he's now armed with another tool to compete in a still-murky Democratic field. 

"The iron is hot for him now, for sure," said Ben Berger, a political scientist at Swarthmore College who leads the school's Lang Center for Civic & Social Responsibility. "It's his moment."

Ahead of Tuesday's midterms, Berger cautioned that Shapiro still has work to do in Pennsylvania to grow support for a presidential run. A Quinnipiac University poll in February found that while 90% of Democrats in Pennsylvania approve of Shapiro's job as governor, only 69% said he would make a good president. Among independents, 49% approved of Shapiro as governor compared with 32% who said he would be a good president. 

"I think people are smart enough to recognize that the governorship is different from the presidency," Berger said. "And so somebody being a good candidate and a good governor — not only a good candidate, but good in the office — doesn't mean they're necessarily going to be good at the next level or be able to win at the next level."

Part of voters' hesitation to endorse Shapiro could stem from a need to see him prove he can carry out his agenda in Pennsylvania. Democrats in Harrisburg are expected to prioritize raising the state's minimum wage, codifying abortion rights, investing in mass transit and legalizing marijuana. Berger also expects to see Shapiro and the legislature formalize the state's rules on data centers after the governor passed an executive order in August to rein in speculative development. 

How much of that platform can be achieved in two years, especially if Shapiro is running for national office, will test the governor's follow-through on promises now that the barrier of Republican obstruction is largely removed. 

History offers many examples of popular governors who won state elections by wide margins but failed to break through in presidential primaries. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and former Ohio Gov. John Kasich both had massive victories before their presidential runs in recent cycles, and former Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis was reelected in a blowout in 1986 before getting crushed by George H.W. Bush in 1988. 

"The only counterexample I can think of, off the top of my head, would be George W. Bush because he had a landslide in Texas in 1998, and that helped to make him the 2000 frontrunner," Berger said.

Early projections for the Democratic field in 2028 include a range of moderate and progressive candidates, including U.S. Sen. John Ossoff of Georgia and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. Former U.S. Transportation Sec. Pete Buttigieg, Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Harris could also run. Newcomers from Tuesday's blue wave could emerge over the coming year as Democrats interpret and build a strategy to leverage their midterm success.

For Shapiro, who has toed the line as a moderate and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, overcoming history could be a limiting factor in a presidential run. No Jewish candidate has ever won a major-party nomination, and Shapiro's strong support for Israel, despite criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, could alienate progressive voters. Shapiro's memoir detailed how Harris' vetting team asked him whether he was an "agent of the Israeli government" before the party ultimately opted for Tim Walz as her running mate. 

"There's going to be, I think, a lot of pressure from the left, and I think it is going to be a liability," Berger said. "Others have moved in the Democratic Party — kind of away from Israel, and he mostly hasn't."

Berger believes Shapiro views the political landscape as a "long game" that will justify throwing his hat into the presidential race, even if he doesn't get the nomination. He could be tapped as a vice presidential candidate or be offered an attractive cabinet position, which would force him to reckon with his political future and his legacy as governor if Democrats take the White House. Sometimes presidential hopefuls who fail early — John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon, for example — come back stronger and win. 

"I think (Shapiro is) probably somebody who will try for it because he knows he's got some heat," Berger said. "I just think it's the case that he's likely not to make it through because of those issues, but I don't think that's likely to be the the end for him."
news.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is widely thought to be weighing a presidential run in 2028. With Democrats' wave of midterm races, Shapiro has momentum to carry out his agenda and build his national profile.

news.title: The moment Donald Trump blew the midterms
news.text:
Democrats just partied like it’s 1974. On Tuesday night, they pulled off the largest midterm victory since the post-Watergate wave. Democratic Senate candidates conquered longtime Republican strongholds like Kansas and Texas — and probably (in the view of the internet’s gamblers) Mississippi and Alaska. When the dust settles, and all ballots are tallied, Democrats are expected to boast a 13-percentage-point popular vote victory and more than 250 House seats.
Taken together, these results exceeded many Democrats’ wildest dreams — and Republicans’ greatest fears. Countless Americans are therefore asking: How the hell did that happen?
To make some headway on that question, I spoke with the Democratic data scientist David Shor. Founder of the consultancy Blue Rose Research, Shor has access to volumes of large-sample polling, precinct-level data on which voters did (and did not) turn out in multiple states, and fine-grained estimates of demographic shifts in party allegiances. 
Historically, Shor has been one of the Democrats’ most prominent Cassandras. For years, he has warned that his party’s falling support among working-class voters threatened to make Democratic Senate majorities a thing of the past. 

Key takeaways
* Democratic turnout surged, particularly among young, politically disengaged, and Latino voters.
* The Iran war was President Donald Trump’s downfall.
* Campaign donors have weird priorities and issue positions, which can undermine politicians who take their money.
* Polling is getting harder.
* Americans think AI might take their jobs and kill their families.

So, I wanted to ask him about the story that his numbers are now telling — and whether it challenges his past assumptions about how American politics works.
On Wednesday afternoon, we also discussed shifts in youth turnout, why Elon Musk’s money bought Republicans so little, and Americans’ growing contempt for artificial intelligence, among other things. Our conversation has been edited for clarity and length. 
What happened Tuesday night? How did Democrats end up with the biggest landslide in half a century?
It’s early; a lot of precincts haven’t come in and we only have individual-level data in a couple of places. But Democrats appear to be running about 7 points ahead of where Kamala Harris was [in 2024].
And it seems like a very large portion of that was due to turnout. You can see this in both the precinct and county-level data. But we also have data on individual voters in Texas and Georgia. And in those two places, Harris supporters turned out at a rate about 9 points higher than Trump supporters did. That’s likely the largest turnout advantage going back to at least 2006. For context, the gap in 2018 was about 3 points.
And a lot of that was young voters. It’s funny; in 2022, everyone said there was a “youthquake” — a huge spike in youth turnout — which was overstated. But this time, one genuinely happened. In Georgia and Texas, there was an enormous increase in youth turnout and actual declines in turnout among voters over 65.
[Image: https://platform.vox.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/shor1.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
We also have evidence that Democrats gained ground with politically disengaged voters. In the precincts that had the lowest turnout rates in 2022, Democrats gained something like 11 points. Whereas the highest turnout precincts swung toward us by only 2 or 3 points. 
It’s a little hard to distinguish changes in support from changes in turnout. But it’s clear that young voters, Hispanic voters, and infrequent voters swung toward us, reversing much of the gains that Republicans made with those groups in 2024.
How big was the increase in Black turnout? Looking at Democrats’ remarkable success in South Carolina and Mississippi, it seems like African American mobilization must have been a factor. 
In the Georgia data, we see a 4-percentage-point increase in the Black share of the electorate relative to 2022, which is quite a bit. And in Texas, we see a nearly 6-percentage-point increase in the Latino share of the electorate. 
What explains these shifts in turnout and voting patterns?
If you look at Trump approval — both from 2016 to 2020 and then from 2024 until the end of 2025 — it was really quite stable. Obviously, it was highest at the beginning of his terms and went down after a month or two. But then for most of Trump’s first term, he was hovering around the mid-40s in our data and it really barely moved in response to events. And it was much the same for the first year of Trump’s second term. Which was worrisome: Trump had all of these scandals, but at the end of the day, the line didn’t move. A good day would be like, “Oh, Trump approval is down three-tenths of a percentage point — amazing!”
So, a lot of people became very nihilistic. They were like, “Oh, we really live in this world where nothing matters.” 
But then, the Iran war happened. And there was a giant structural shift in public opinion. His approval rating on the cost of living plummeted. To put some numbers on this, the day before the Iran war, Donald Trump had a 49 percent approval rating on gas prices. Within a week, it was 33 percent. 
[Image: https://platform.vox.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/shor2.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Trump’s overall approval rating isn’t that much lower than in 2018. And his approval on immigration, healthcare, and a lot of other issues is pretty similar. The big change in our polling has been a giant decline in Trump’s approval on the economy. 
And previously, voters’ trust in his economic management was the one thing propping him up. But the Iran war destroyed it. And he went from being a complicated political figure — who was popular on the economy but unpopular on other things — to being unpopular on everything. 
So, Tuesday’s wave had less to do with what Democrats did right than what Republicans did wrong? Are there portable lessons here for Democrats besides, “When a GOP president engineers a massive increase in gas prices, tell voters you disapprove?”
I’m not going to claim that the Democratic brand is perfect. But I think the Democratic leadership and both wings of the Democratic Party — the left and the “establishment” or whatever — deserve a lot of credit for making big, concrete shifts in their messaging; specifically, focusing more on economic issues that affect people’s everyday lives. That was not a given. It was not uncontroversial at the time. And it paid dividends. 
Right before the 2024 election, Republicans had a 12-point trust advantage on the cost of living. Today, among 2026 voters, Democrats actually have the trust advantage on the issue, which continues to be voters’ No. 1 concern by far. 
We ask voters questions like, “What do you think the Democratic Party cares about?” And when we asked that question a year after the 2024 election, voters thought Democrats prioritized catering to their base over the cost of living by 4 to 1.
When we ran that survey again right before this year’s election, voters thought Democrats cared about the cost of living more than anything else, just like them. They thought Democrats’ second concern was fighting Donald Trump, which maybe wasn’t a total positive. But then No. 3 was healthcare and No. 4 was the economy. And so Democrats really did execute a big pivot.
And meanwhile, if you ask voters what they think that Trump cares about, they say border security, immigration, national security, and war in the Middle East. You have to go far down the list to get to costs. 
The other thing I’d say for Democratic strategy: The 2025 government shutdown did damage Trump.
Until then, Trump really felt like he had escalation dominance, that basically every time he would violate norms and trigger a fight, he felt — based on previous experience — that he would win and that Democrats would have to back down. And this was the first high-profile fight between Democrats and Trump where he really paid a big price and his approval started to go down.
And I think that partly reflects Democrats choosing to center the shutdown on healthcare, one of the issues voters really cared about. There were a lot of people in the Democratic Party who wanted to focus on other things, for understandable reasons. But if you look at the postmortem, the healthcare shutdown corresponded with a massive increase in the salience of healthcare in the minds of voters. And that correspondingly led to an increase in support for Democrats and disapproval of Trump.
In our past conversations, you often painted a pretty bleak picture of the Democratic Party’s prospects for winning control of the Senate. And not without reason. 
In the last few elections, it seemed like moderate Democratic candidates were having a harder and harder time competing in Republican-leaning states. Which was a problem, since Democrats couldn’t win control of the Senate without prevailing in states that voted for Trump every chance they got. 
And you argued that Democrats’ problem was structural: Voters increasingly got their political information from national outlets, which focused on the big-picture ideological divides between the two parties rather than the idiosyncratic positioning of individual candidates. Culturally conservative Montana voters realized that voting for Jon Tester meant empowering social liberals. And so Democrats were kind of screwed, unless they found a way to moderate their national image.
And yet, the national Democratic Party didn’t really moderate any of its issue positions between 2024 and 2026 — yet still managed to win statewide elections in Kansas, Iowa, and probably Alaska and Mississippi. So, how do you reconcile these results with your model of political reality?
I’m a little more wary of making long-term predictions than I was in my 20s. Obviously, I would have been shocked in 2019 if you had told me how many Senate seats we would have today. But it’s worth walking through what happened, year by year.
What’s interesting about 2022 and 2024 is that we really should have lost a lot of races, in many different senses. What saved us is that, in both those years, Democrats had a historic advantage in candidate quality — measured by objective things like, “Was this person elected to a previous office?” 
And if you really drill into individual details, this was largely because Trump intervened in swing-state primaries in the House and Senate to support lower-quality candidates who were loyal to him.
One mathematical way to see this is to look at how Democrats in swing races did relative to Democrats in non-swing races. And in 2014 and 2018, the gap was basically zero. But in 2022, it was something like 3 percent. And then in 2024, it was a little bit more muted, but similar. 
So, I think Republicans were on the cusp of securing a level of power in American politics that no party had experienced in decades. But Trump spent down that power to accomplish his goals. I definitely didn’t see that coming. 
As for this election, I did not predict that Trump would start a super unpopular war while also doing massive tariffs and making a bunch of other domestic political miscalculations.
I have two takeaways from all this. The first is I think that political parties have a real tendency towards equilibrating behavior, where in response to having lots of seats, they go and do a bunch of politically counterproductive things.
The other piece is: In the past, I had said that it was impossible to hold the Senate without Democrats winning culturally conservative voters in states that backed Trump by large margins.
And that continues to be true. The question was, “Is it possible for us to get there?” At the time, I think a lot of people really thought that these levels of overperformance were impossible. But it turns out there are different paths to getting there, and one is having the president launch a giant unpopular war, while doing everything he can to drive down his own approval rating.
What do you think this election tells us about the power of money in politics? The GOP had a financial advantage this cycle. And yet, at first glance, it doesn’t look like Elon Musk’s $445 million investment in Republican power made much of a difference. 
Obviously money does matter. Ads do work. It’s not like these effects are zero. But as the amount of money in politics has increased, political parties have started catering enormously to the whims of donors who are really quite weird. 
In our issue priorities polling, the cost of living is the top issue for every subgroup imaginable — young voters, Hispanic voters, Black voters, old voters, whatever. Every single group, except for the 0.7 percent of the population that has donated to a Democratic campaign in the last year. And for them, climate change is No. 1, voting rights is No. 2, you have to go down to like 11 or something to get to the cost of living. And I think that explains a lot about elite Democrats’ behavior historically.
So, it’s better to be outspent and in touch with the American voter than it is to be the opposite. I like to say: Whichever party listens less to their donors usually wins. 
You can’t blame donors for everything in the Trump presidency — tariffs were probably all him — but if you look at what he did, his donors pushed him to take incredibly unpopular positions on AI and on data centers. 
After Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, Trump said that no new AI regulations were needed. We polled that statement. And it was literally the most unpopular position I’ve ever seen a mainstream politician endorse. About 8 percent of people supported it. That’s three times less popular than defunding the police.
Holding all else equal, more money is helpful. But if getting it requires you to spend 70 to 80 percent of your time talking to some of the weirdest people on the planet — and forces you to prioritize issues that the general public doesn’t care about — you’re better off with less money. 
Zohran Mamdani is an example of this. He showed that if you single-mindedly focus your campaign on voters’ top issue — affordability — you can really do incredible things, while your opponents are wasting time arguing about Israel.
Why did the polls underestimate Democrats so significantly? In some recent elections, polls had tended to overestimate Democrats, particularly in redder areas. And you argued this was because voters with low social trust had become both less likely to answer a pollster’s call — and more likely to support Republicans. And that led pollsters to systematically undercount Trump voters. But this time, the miss went in the other direction. 
We’re still trying to piece together exactly what the data says. But the fundamental problem in polling is that the two biggest predictors of answering a phone survey are: 1) how interested you are in politics and 2) your socioeconomic status — as measured not only by education and income, but also things that are much harder for survey takers to gauge, like, “How educated were your parents?” or “What’s the occupational prestige of your job?” or “What kind of neighborhood do you live in?”
In 2012, a voter’s level of interest in politics wasn’t super correlated with support for Obama or Romney. But now they are.
And technology is part of why. If you go back to the 1950s, if someone received a call from a pollster, they’d be like, “Oh my God, there’s a researcher who wants to know my views on contemporary events!” and they would excitedly drop what they’re doing and talk to them. But now there is a multitrillion-dollar war for people’s attention. And so it is in fact quite hard to get non-random samples of people excited to take that call. That problem isn’t going away. So I expect more polling misses in the future.
How do you interpret the variation in Democratic performance between states? Democratic Senate candidates in Texas and Iowa vastly outperformed Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins, while those in Maine and Michigan did so more modestly. How much of that gap is driven by demographics — Trump simply induced a backlash among specific groups that are more present in some states than in others — versus candidate quality? And to the extent that candidate quality was important, did that boil down to ideological positioning or more intangible assets?
We did a big survey right before the election where we asked voters, “How moderate do you think this candidate is?” And then we also asked a bunch of other questions like, “How much do you think this person cares about economic issues?” “How in touch are they with the economic struggles that everyday people face?” 
And we found that perceived moderation is associated with higher vote share. Though I think in the House, these effects are smaller than a lot of people would guess. What’s more interesting, though, is it really seems like the extent to which voters see you as focused on economic issues — and in touch with what regular people care about — is much more predictive of overperformance than ideology.
And I think that if you go and look at individual politicians, there are lots of examples of both progressive and moderate politicians who are perceived as out of touch. 
And I think the left is learning this. If you look at the ideological penalty that candidates supported by Justice Democrats have paid each election cycle, they’ve gone down over time, as these groups have matured a bit and focused on economic messaging. 
One big story from Tuesday night was the massive backlash to data center construction. Forty out of 41 ballot proposals for restricting data centers passed. What do you make of that? In your polling, is this opposition driven primarily by concerns about the structures themselves — their appearance, pollution, and impact on local energy bills? Or is it primarily an outlet for voters to express their antipathy for AI as a technology? 
Over the last two years, voters have grown increasingly concerned about AI. In 2024, AI ranked 40th out of 40 on our list of voter priorities. But it’s gained salience by more than any other issue since the start of Trump’s presidency; now it’s ranked 24th out of 39, roughly tied with crime. 
And as that salience has increased, people have become increasingly negative about AI. In December of last year, we asked people whether they were more optimistic or pessimistic about AI, and optimism led by about 5 points. In our most recent polling, pessimism leads by 10 points.
Late last year, when we asked, “Do you want a data center built in your neighborhood?” we saw 45 percent support. In our polling a month or two ago, that fell to 14 percent. For context, when you ask voters whether they want a prison in their neighborhood, that figure is 15 percent. 
And obviously, part of that is NIMBY concerns. But I think that this is part and parcel of AI becoming more unpopular. 
And I think it’s impossible to understand why AI is unpopular without considering voters’ views on the broader economy. Consumer confidence is roughly at the level it was right after the Great Recession. Ask people, “Do you think the economy is rigged for elites or are things fair?” People say “rigged.” Ask, “Do you trust our business elites?” People overwhelmingly say no. And these are very big changes from before the pandemic. 
So, if you believe the country’s elites cannot be trusted — and then you also hear a bunch of business people saying, “AI is going to change everything!” — it’s natural to assume that change is going to screw you. 
And in fact, 80 percent of voters say it’s either very likely or somewhat likely that there will be large-scale job loss due to AI in the next five years. And something like 64 percent say it’s either very likely or somewhat likely that AI will threaten human survival. So the median voter thinks that there is a considerable chance that AI will take their job and kill their family.
If America’s tech elites really want this large-scale build out and reorganization of the economy to happen, they will have to actually pressure Congress to meaningfully protect the downside risks of the American people and guarantee them some share of AI’s upside. Because, as we saw yesterday, we live in a democracy. And the American people will not allow this AI transition to happen unless they get something for it.
